description:
A scrappy expanse of silky refuges and capture webs littered with body parts of previous victims. When preferred prey is entangled, the female spiders emerge from their 'nests' and overpower it by grabbing its extremities. In this case, a wasp https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/9319446. 
Presumably they inject venom because after a minute or so the prey stops struggling. Then they snip it out of the web and carry it into one of several 'nests' or refuges.
 Unwanted prey, often beetles (see https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/9319435 ) are also killed but sometimes left in the web, uneaten.  Ants, in this case, Maranoplus ( https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/9319390 )scavenge around the periphery of the webs, feasting on unwanted beetles or other left-overs.

description: There once was a Western Whiptail Lizard making its home around my house. On early Monday mornings, trash days, I moved the blue bin very carefully to the curb because the lizard spent the nights under it. Sometimes it made its way into my garage. Yesterday it jumped out of an empty flower pot as I walked by. Each time I saw it I grabbed the camera hoping it would allow me to take a picture. No such luck. It was a very, very shy lizard. I was working away on the computer and heard unusual amounts of rustling in the dry leaves under the shrubs in front of my window. I jumped up and looked -- into the eyes of a Greater Roadrunner, holding the Western Whiptail Lizard in its beak. I was thinking, oh no, the poor Lizzie, but admittedly, also feeling a little excited, and happy for the Roadrunner to have found a meal. I'm sure you all know what I'm talking about, these mixed feelings and the heartbreak when nature isn't all cute kitten pix. The Roadrunner took its prey to the street and smashed it onto the asphalt, over and over again. This gave me a moment to find the camera and sneak outside and take a few hectic pictures...   (Western Whiptail observation: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/14271438)

description:
7 part photostory, this one is for the fly
Photo 1:
 I Thought It Was A Yellowjacket
When I came inside my house, what I thought was a yellow jacket came in with me.  This is a problem because I like to go barefoot and I have cats that could get stung also.  I went to get a broom to try to slap it down out of the air.  When I came back it had gone to a window with blinds.  I discovered that a tiny spider had solved my problem.  The "yellow jacket" had been caught in a web.  Later when I got the insect identified by experts, it turned out to be a fly pretending to be a yellow jacket.  This is an example of Batesian mimicry which is when a harmless, tasty species mimics another species that is toxic or foul tasting or dangerous in order to be protected from predators.  Sure fooled me.  It did not deter the spider.
Photo 2:
Spider To The Rescue
The spider solved my problem.  Here is the spider coming to take a look at what it caught in its web.  I was shooting these photos through open blinds.
Photo 3:
Underside Of The Spider
I took this shot to help with getting an id on the spider.
Photo 4:
Topside Of The Spider
As the spider wrapped some silk around the fly's legs, I got a shot of the top side of the spider. 
Photo 5:
Uncropped Shot For Perspective
I left this shot uncropped to show how I was having to do this, shooting between two blinds slats.     
Photo 6:
Spider Injects venom
The spider may have been fooled by the mimicry because it avoided the end of the fly where a stinger would be if it were a wasp.  What the spider did, as shown here, was to bite the leg which injected venom.  The fly stopped struggling shortly after that.
Photo 7:
The Spider Won
I had to leave at this point so took this last photo of the spider.  Several hours later when I got back the fly was wrapped up in silk for a later meal.  The next morning there was nothing left to be seen.
Fly  id confirmed in bugguide here:  https://bugguide.net/node/view/1616641

description: This large bee fly was found in close association with a colony of alkali bees (Halictidae), Nomia nortoni. (The fly is a parasitoid of the bee.) The fly resembles genus Bombylius, but note the curved (sinuate) rear edge of the eye--in Bombylius this is nearly straight. When posted on BugGuide originally, this was the first record for North Carolina, and there has been just one other record from that state since on BugGuide. It may have been the first record overall for the state, as I did not see any records at that time on the NCSU entomology online collection, nor in Brimley's Insects of North Carolina (1938). The fly is widespread in the western United States, but its distribution in the east is spotty. I keep meaning to go up to this site again to see if I can find the bees and the flies--maybe I will make it this year! Bomber Fly - Heterostylum robustum bugguide.net/node/view/76992 Original BugGuide posting of fly: bugguide.net/node/view/76558/ This is a female--the male has eyes touching over the top of the head (holoptic). Update 8/23/24. I added some detail images showing the margin of the eye and the wing venation.

A few minutes ago, I spotted a green anole hunting in an area where frostweeds, yellow passionflowers, and late bonesets are blooming and attracting a variety of bees, wasps, and flies.  In picture 1, there is a fly on a late bonset bloom just below the lizard.  In the left corner, there is a wasp barely visible in the late boneset.  On the yellow passionflower bloom, there is a small red-banded hairstreak. Picture 2 is a closeup of the hunter.  Picture 3 shows that it now has locked on to the hairstreak as a target. Picture 4  shows the lizard patiently getting ready.  Picture 5 and 6 were taken just before the lizard pounced on its prey.  Pictures 7, 8, and 9 show the lizard after it has captured the hairstreak and moves about with the hairstreak in its mouth.

One or more of these frogs hang out in my wife's herb garden which provides cover, moisture, and a plentiful supply of insects for the frog(s) to eat.  Also hanging around in the same small garden is a larger Southern leopard frog.  More often than not, the frogs disappear quickly when I try to photograph them, but in this case the frog remained still while chomping down on a fly.

As I was taking a picture of this female Common Merganser (Gänsesäger) in the channel at the entry of Nymphenburg Palace, she suddenly raced away with her bill and eyes under water. I first thought she was chasing Black-headed Gulls, but she surfaced with a Chub that was so large and heavy that she lost her grip on it. She must have stunned the fish, because she pulled it out again after searching for it under water. This time, she didn’t only struggle with the weight of the fish, she was also surrounded by excited Gulls who wanted to get a bite. I even had to back up at one point, because it walked inside the focus range of my camera.

description:
I was wondering what they were doing around the gate post, since it didn't look like they were actually going into a nest. Then I noticed the ants:
https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/96841068

Apparently they were waiting for the larger winged ones to come up (3rd pic.). They would then grab these and carry them off to feed their larva. 
Lots of photos to show the action, including the little ants trying to fight back (pic. 11).

There were several yellojackets flying around the base of the gate post and I was wondering what they were doing.
Apparently they were waiting for the larger winged ants coming up to go off and start new colonies. The yellowjackets would then grab these and carry them off to feed their larva. Not many got away, but for some reason there was a few minutes where the yellowjackets disappeared and a few were able to fly off, and I got to get a bit closer for these pictures. 

See the yellowjacket listing for more photos here:
https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/96841067

There was also a lizzard that appeared to be waiting for a chance to grab some too, while avoiding the wasps.
https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/96841066

I came across the pair apparently shortly after the snake had bitten the toad, around 14:30. In the video the adder can be seen giving the toad a second bite.
The snake started swallowing the toad at 14:38, the toad still struggling strongly. The toad stopped moving at around 14:41.
Initially I started filming on my phone as the snake was blocking the path to my camera and I didn't want to disturb it. An hour in (15:30), it was apparent that the snake was untroubled by the various humans and cats watching it, and I swapped to the camera.
By 16:50 the snake had swallowed the toad up to its hips. At 17:16 it partially regurgitated the prey and started swallowing again.
At 17:36 it again regurgitated a large portion of the toad - its front legs and feet were visible.
At 17:56 only the back legs were still protruding.
The toad was completely swallowed at 18:09, 3.5 hours in all.
The video (3mins 30 sec) is edited and speeded up 2x.

I took one cell phone shot inside, then took my camera outside to get some unobstructed images. I could just reach it by climbing up too high on a stepstool braced against the wall. The background (window) was far too dark. Aha, I had faced this issue before. I taped a piece of white paper on the *inside* of the window behind the fly and got a nice clean background. I had fun playing with different lighting. Adjacent images/observation highlights the prey, a (edit) flesh fly--Sarcophagidae. I’d been watching my woods because of the dead opossum [ https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/150086636 ] I’d moved there.  Nothing amiss when walking out there 3/6/2023.  Morning of 3/7, from my window I saw red among the brown leaves.  With binos, I saw a big streak of bright red blood and a rib cage, then a coyote carrying something out of my sight.  The red blood had completely faded away within a half hour, which indicated to me the kill had been relatively recent.  Morning of 3/8, I ventured out and found where a young deer had been taken apart all over the place and (presumably) other creatures had been picking it clean.  My guess is that coyote(s) had pounced on the deer where it had bedded down for the night.  The dead opossum was untouched.

Since the discovery of the Cionus pupa covered in soil, https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/191465167  I re-read something that @beetledude wrote , viz, "Keep a look out for their remarkable cocoons. They produce a unique, opaque, thin-parchment-like "bubble" inside which the pupa is housed. These cocoons are also attached to the outside of the hostplant, often on leaves." (https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/9177433)
And @borisb wrote: "btw: These pupate in tiny, globular cocoons attached to plant (rare in weevils)".
(https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/191465167)

So I wondered, why then, when we sit under a Buddleja, we get pelted with little sticky larvae apparently flinging themselves from the tree?
I put 6 larvae in 4 containers, on Buddleja sprigs. Soil was either piled in one quarter of the floor space or covered the floor. The pupae were located as follows:
2 attached to leaves;
2 were lying on top of the soil;
2 had attached themselves to the bare plastic on the bottom of the container.

Description

L. rigidum is an annual species forming open tussocks. The dominant habit is erect, but the species is variable in habit, ranging from dense prostrate to more open erect types. Geniculate stems, fibrous root system, up to 1 m high. Reddish-purple colouration at base of stems extends upwards as the plant matures. Leaf blades dark green, hairless, flat, upper surface evenly ribbed, lower surface smooth and shiny, 5-25 cm long, 3-5 mm wide. Young leaves rolled in bud. Auricles small and narrow. Ligule, white, translucent, shorter than wide. Leaf sheath hairless, with fine longitudinal ribs as in leaf blades, reddish-purple at base. Inflorescence is a spike up to 30 cm in length; spikelets edge on to the rachis. Rachis is recessed opposite each spikelet, which more or less fits into the recess. Spikelets of 10-12 florets, laterally flattened, green, 10-25 mm long. Only the terminal spikelet has two more or less equal glumes. Otherwise only one glume subtending each spikelet, lanceloate, 10-15 mm long, two-thirds to three-quarters as long as the spikelet, outer surface fine-veined, ribbed like the upper surface of the leaf blade. No awn. Lemma lanceolate, about 5 mm long, five nerved, usually with no awn, but terminal awns occasionally found, probably as a result of hybridization. Palea similar to lemma in shape and size, two nerves with tiny hairs along them. Anthers three, yellow.

Erstmals systematisch beschrieben wurde die Bambusmilbe 1917 unter dem lateinischen Namen Stigmaeopsis celarius. 1950 wurde die Art neu beschrieben und der Gattung Schizotetranychus angegliedert. Vor kurzem allerdings wurde die Gattung Stigmaeopsis – aufgrund detaillierter molekularbiologischer und morphologischer Studien – wieder allein gestellt (Saito et al., 2004). So far, in Europe, two species of alien tetranychid 
mites have been recorded on bamboos, namely Stigmaeopsis celarius Banks in The Netherlands, Great 
Britain, Belgium and France, and Schizotetranychus 
bambusae Reck in France only (Vierbergen, 1997; 
Ostoja-Starzewski, 2000; Auger and Migeon, 2007). S. 
celarius is also widespread in the USA. 
Presently, the S. celarius complex consists of seven 
species: S. celarius, S. nanjingensis, S. longus (Saito), S. 
miscanthi (Saito), (the last two previously known as celarius in Japan), S. tenuinidis (Zhang et Zhang), S. saharai Saito et Mori and S. takahashi Saito et Mori, (Saito et al., 2004). Of these, only S. miscanthi inhabits plants other than bamboo.

Presently S. nanjingensis is widespread in the Veneto Region (North-Eastern Italy) on ornamental bamboos (Phyllostachys mitis, P. nigra and, to a less extent, Pseudosasa japonica). Infestations were observed in Padua, Treviso and Vicenza districts, both in new and old plantations of historical parks. Moreover it has been recorded also in the Liguria region (North-western Italy), at Ventimiglia (Imperia district), near the French border. Die 8 untersuchten Bambusmilbenarten der Gattung Stigmaeopsis unterscheiden sich unter anderem in der Art des Nestbaues und in der sozialen Organisation. Dabei treten zwei Extreme auf. Zum einem gibt es Arten, die – wie die bei uns eingescheppten Bambusmilben (Stigmaeopsis nanjingensis oder Stigmaeopsis longus) – große, aneinanderhängende Nester mit vielen Individuen bauen, welche beim Gegenangriff auf Räuber zusammenarbeiten können. Zum anderen gibt es Arten, die das Risiko eines Angriffs durch Räuber reduzieren, indem sie verstreut liegende kleine und feste Nester bauen, die nur mit größerem Aufwand aufgestöbert werden können und in welche die Räuber nur schlecht eindringen können. Die Individuen dieser Arten zeigen keinen Gegenangriff.



Daneben gibt es auch interessante Zwischen- bzw. Sonderformen des Nestbaus, auf die ich hier jedoch nicht näher eingehen möchte.



Interessant ist vielleicht noch, dass die Milben ihr Nest nicht mit ihren schlecht entwickelten Augen erkennen, sondern mithilfe bestimmter Borsten auf dem Rücken ertasten. Milbenarten mit größeren Borsten bauen auch größere Nester.

1. Ein einzelner Ablageplatz innerhalb des Nestes (Stigmaeopsis nanjingensis)

3. Zwei Ablageplätze außerhalb des Nestes
4. Mehrere Ablageplätze in unmittelbarer Nähe der Nestöffnungen
5. Weit entfernt von den Nestöffnungen wahllos verteilte Ablageplätze

The characteristics most general ly useful in the iden til leat ion of bamboo species (once the genus is known) are found i n the culm sheaths that clothe the young shoot. These characteristics reveal themselves most vividly while the sheaths are in a fresh state. As they dry, their delicate, ol ten very distinctive colors fade to light or dark straw, though any spots of dark pigment usually persist. The tissues shrink and sometimes become more or less warped, and some of the delicate parts, such as the auricles and the ligule, become brittle and easily broken when dry.
https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/9307821

The most useful single organ is the culm sheath. But an adequate specimen should include examples (from the same culm if possible) representing the basal, middle, ~and upper part of the series, and so labelled. Next in importance for purposes of identification (when used in conjunction with the culm sheaths) are specimens of the lower one or two meters of the mature culm itself. The branch complement, and internodes within the branched part of the culm, are principally useful for generic identifications. Finally, the more completely the specimen represents the plant, and the more adequate the supplementary notes, the more reliable the identification may be.

description: Flower scarab - Valgus canaliculatus (males, ~5 mm) These were all over the persimmon flowers, often disappearing most of the way down into the flower. I have usually found them on Viburnum previously. These always remind me of ticks. Genus name is Latin valgus, "bow-legged". These are canaliculatus (versus V. seticollis), based on: - dark reddish brown (vs. piceous) - anterior tibiae with 3 slender, widely-separated teeth on outer side (vs. 5-6) - pronotum with many small teeth along edge (vs. large teeth) - overlapping cream-colored scales on abdominal sternites (vs. non-overlapping, tawny); visible in one image Female of canaliculatus has long process on pygidium, lacking here, so these should be males. It seems that primarily males visit flowers (Ratclifee and Paulsen). The species is termetophilous--eggs, larvae, and adults can be found in the galleries of Reticulitermes flavipes (several references below). References - BugGuide bugguide.net/node/view/5242 - Dillon and Dillon, A Manual of Common Beetles of Eastern North America (Row, Peterson, and Company, 1961), p. 558, plate 53(16) - Evans, Beetles of Eastern North America (Princeton University Press, 2014), p. 177 - Harpootlian, Scarab Beetles of South Carolina (Clemson University, 2001), p. 124, figs. 243, 285 - Ratcliffe and Jameson, Generic Guide to New World Scarabs unsm-ento.unl.edu/Guide/Scarabaeoidea/Scarabaeidae/Cetoni... - Ratcliffe and Paulsen, The Scarabaeoid Beetles of Nebraska (Bulletin of the University of Nebraska State Museum, Vol 22, 2008), pp. 503-4, fig. 688

description:
Nature is metal, as they say.

There were tons of gulls and blackbirds at Kings Beach today. And there were tons of people watching and photographing the gulls. But nobody seemed to be paying much attention to the blackbirds which, I guess, is to be expected. But that was unfortunate for them because when blackbirds scatter and/or fly off in a flock, it's worth taking a closer look.

As I walked past a tree filled with blackbirds, their chatter increased and they quickly bolted. I looked up and saw one bigger bird amongst the crowd. Sure enough, a Peregrine Falcon swooped in for some takeout!

Within seconds, the Peregrine Falcon had caught, killed, and flew off with its lunch. Crazy fast and I'm willing to bet that I was the only person to even notice. Even in a developed area such as this, awesome nature interactions are taking place!

Alice Herden told me about the first stop; a recent burn with thousands of Liatris stalks. Unfortuntely, we did not see many native arthropods (but Western Honeybees were common). I don't think I had ever seen so many treefroggies (including many Pinewoods Treefrogs)!

These are my cell-phone images, which are GPS-enabled. In some cases, I am uploading a cell-phone image just to have the precise location, and I will later upload my (superior) camera images.

description: With Don Fraser, Clint Gibson, Shelley Rutkin, and Liz Childress; a successful chase of two rare bees. We found _Colletes banksi_ pollening on Dahoon Holly (_Ilex cassine_) -- a new food plant -- and we found several _Melissodes mitchelli_, the star of the show. According to Clint (who knows these things), mitchelli had not been identifiable photographed in the wild previously! It all started on 12 April 2025, when Don, Clint, and I participated in the Annuteliga Hammock butterfly count. During the count, I saw a bee gathering pollen from a prickly pear cactus. I took one cell-phone photograph then the bee was gone. Later, I showed Clint the photo, and he said that could be a real good bee, _Melissodes mitchelli_, which is a Florida endemic, is exclusive to prickly pear pollen ("oligolectic"), and is known from just a few records, all of them specimens. It turns out that Don had photographed probably the same bee last year at Chassahowitzka Wildlife and Environmental Area on a trip with me and Alice Herden. Then, Cliff and his wife found and collected a male _Melissodes mitchelli_ (Clint has permits ...) at Starkey Wilderness Preserve on 17 April 2025. So the stage was set for this day at Chassahowitzka. Clint found and captured (but did not collect) a _Melissodes mitchelli_, which we all photographed before Clint released it. We started out on Rattlesnake Camp Road and then drove Scrub Island Road. Finally, we drove 3 Bridge Road to the sandhills area at the northern edge of the property. I took my first photographs at 1055 and my last at 1539. The weather at the start was sunny, 84 degrees ("feels like" 85), and with SW winds at 9 MPH.

description:
Some old pictures I found of when my chickens were playing keep away with a dead sparrow. I'm not sure if they found it dead or managed to kill it or how long they'd had it, but it was pretty beaten up since they had thrown it around and pecked holes in its chest.

They were all very keen to eat it so they were constantly stealing it from one another and running away with it. I took a few pictures and then chased them down to get it back since I didn't want them eating another bird especially since I didn't know how it died. They were very reluctant to give it up and devastated when they weren't allowed to eat it.

House sparrows were common in our yard when we had chickens since they loved the chicken scratch feed. They would feed very close to the chickens so I don't doubt that they would be able to grab one not paying attention. The sparrow also potentially hit the window and the chickens took advantage of it being stunned or killed.

Reporting to dbird.

Quoting from the original Facebook post containing additional video 🎥 footage: https://www.facebook.com/share/p/16BKMTU7Tf/

Wow! We weren't expecting this! 😮

We've often seen these tiny metallic green flies here in Gulu, but this is the first time we've seen one apparently eating another teeny winged insect! Who would have known?

The green fly is a Long-Legged Fly, Dolichopodidae sp.: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/68020-Dolichopodidae, and possibly a member of the Chrysosomatini tribe: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6986&subview=map&taxon_id=1309119&view=species and: https://www.facebook.com/groups/Butterfliesandbugs/permalink/6966382546792519/?app=fbl. Thanks for confirming the ID Johan Pretorius 🙂

"Dolichopodidae, the long-legged flies, are a large, cosmopolitan family of true flies with more than 8,000 described species in about 250 genera. The genus Dolichopus is the most speciose, with some 600 species.

Dolichopodidae generally are small flies with large, prominent eyes and a metallic cast to their appearance, though there is considerable variation among the species. Most have long legs, though some do not. In many species, the males have unusually large genitalia which are taxonomically useful in identifying species. Most adults are predatory on other small animals, though some may scavenge or act as kleptoparasites of spiders or other predators. 

Dolichopodidae are a family of flies ranging in size from minute to medium-sized (1 mm to 9 mm). They have characteristically long and slender legs, though their leg length is not as striking as in families such as the Tipulidae. Their posture often is stilt-like standing high on their legs, with the body almost erect. In colour most species have a green-to-blue metallic lustre, but various other species are dull yellow, brown or black...

In most species the mouthparts are short and have a wide aperture as an adaptation for sucking small prey...

Adults of the Dolichopodidae live largely in grassy places and shrubbery. The flies occur in a wide range of habitats, near water or in meadows, woodland edges and in gardens. Some groups are confined to wet places including sands on the banks of water bodies; examples include genera such as Porphyrops, Tachytrechus, Campsicnemus, and Teuchophorus. No truly aquatic species have been described, but many are semi-aquatic and live in or near water margins. A small number of species develop on the shores of saline inland bodies of water or the intertidal zone of seashores. An example of a species that develop close to water is P. nobilitatus, they can be found congregating around lakes and ponds. Other groups are found on trunks of trees damaged by bark beetles. Adults often are seen in a characteristic predatory posture standing high on their legs on the ground or on vegetation, tree trunks or rocks, and some species walk about on the surface of still water.

The adults are predators, feeding on small invertebrates including Collembola, aphids, and the larvae of Oligochaeta. Species of the genus Dolichopus commonly prey on the larvae of mosquitoes.

The larvae occupy a wide range of habitats. Many are predators of small invertebrates and generally live in moist environments such as soil, moist sand, or rotting organic matter. Genera such as Medetera live as predators under tree bark or in the tunnels of bark beetles. Larvae of the genus Thrypticus are unusual among Dolichopodidae, in that they are phytophagous and live in the stems of reeds and other monocots near water.

Many studies have shown that Dolichopodidae give visual, rather than chemical or other signals during courtship. The males of many species exhibit elaborate secondary sexual characters assumed to aid in species recognition during courtship. These characters include flaglike flattening of the arista and tarsi, strongly modified setae and projections of the tarsi, the prolongation and deformation of podomeres, orientated silvery pruinosity, and maculation or modification of the wings." 

Interestingly Jan Botha commented that he "Saw dolly 1st time in apple orchard feeding on mites (ERM) around 1988, Grabouw." Thanks for sharing about that Jan 🙂

We looked up ERM is and learned a bit more about them from an article by Jim Walgenbach, Extension Entomology Specialist (Fruits/Vegetables) Entomology, "European Red Mite": https://content.ces.ncsu.edu/european-red-mite-1

"European red mite (Panonychus ulmi; ERM) is found on fruit trees, shade trees, and shrubs worldwide. It is the most common mite occurring on apple trees...

ERM feed on leaves. When populations are severe, leaves may lose color or become brown (a condition referred to as "bronzing"). This can lead to fewer fruit, dropped fruit, and lower fruit quality, as well as a lower return bloom the following season.

Many factors determine the severity of a mite infestation, including the time of year when injury occurs, the duration of feeding, the trees' vigor and cultivar, crop load, and weather conditions."

There's another interesting article by Ricky E. Foster, Extension Entomologist, "Fruit Insects EUROPEAN RED MITE MANAGEMENT": https://extension.entm.purdue.edu/publications/E-258/E-258.html

"Prior to the advent of modern, synthetic insecticides, European red mites (ERM) were not considered a significant pest of tree fruits. ERM are what entomologists call a “secondary pest,” which means that they generally only became a pest in response to some action by people."

It's nice to know we've been having some living biocontrol agents protecting the fruit trees in the garden from mite attacks all along! 😄

As mentioned in our other main mielie post, (https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/283369531) we're delving behind some mielie ears and sharing what we've found.

In the first two videos (see original Facebook post link) we see a brief glimpse of an aphid-farming ant zipping past. The quiet pasture has been discovered! In the second video and third videos the cattle are roaming...there is also a whitish larva (discussed further here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/283499883), squirming right behind the aphid.

What type of aphids could these be? 🤔

Edit: After investigating further, we came to the conclusion none of the current locally-reported aphid species on INaturalist seem to fit, but the Corn Leaf Aphid, Rhopalosiphum maidis does: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/330189-Rhopalosiphum-maidis. "Rhopalosiphum maidis, common names corn leaf aphid and corn aphid, is an insect, and a pest of maize and other crops. It has a nearly worldwide distribution and is typically found in agricultural fields, grasslands, and forest-grassland zones." 

Searching a little further afield we found that the presence of this aphid has indeed been reported on by the South African Agricultural Research Council: https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-sgi/Pages/Crop%20Protection/Insect-pests-of-leaves-and-stems.aspx. Thanks for confirming the ID of these little ones Natalie Hernandez* - much appreciated! 

*Natalie has a B.S. and M.Sc. in Entomology from the University of Wisconsin - Madison (USA) and her graduate research focused on alate aphids.

Inside the mielie leaf...🔎

As mentioned in our other main mielie post, (https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/283369531) we're delving behind some mielie ears and sharing what we've found.

🌍 We previously mentioned some weird buglets in another sub-post: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/283381488.

They move forwards, sideways and even backwards, even at high speed! What an astonishing thing to see! 👀

They seem to come in various colours ranging from white, to grey, to beige, to black. There are various sizes, ranging from teeny-tiny to ant-sized. They also come in various shapes: some look like tiny hoppers, some like miniature accordions, some even look like a finger, complete with a nail (like "Thing" from the Addams Family 👉) and some have wings! Irrespective of colour, size or shape, they *all* behave like tiny basketball players without a ball...😅🤣😂 🏀

Are these possibly several stages of a type of hopper? 

Enjoy!

Edit: Thank you so much Andrew Schild for helping us with this one. It looks as if you have the identification completely right. It does indeed look as if this is a Corn Delphacid, Peregrinus maidis (even though the ones in this post are different in colour than the photos of this species on iNaturalist and there don't seem to be any observations listed for South Africa as yet): https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/330085-Peregrinus-maidis. What an amazing little creature! 

"Peregrinus maidis, commonly known as the corn planthopper, is a species of insect in the order Hemiptera and the family Delphacidae. It is widespread throughout most tropical and subtropical regions on earth...P. maidis are a commercially important pest of maize and its relatives." 

"P. maidis demonstrate sexual dimorphism in body size between males and females. Males have a body length of 2mm with a 6mm wingspan, whereas females are slightly larger at 3mm long and 7mm wingspan."

"The species thrives in low elevation, high humidity locations and populations will decrease at altitudes above 800m. It is suspected that P. maidis cannot move into higher latitudes due to an inability to overwinter. P. maidis are thought to have originated in Australia as a pest of sorghum but quickly spread with the widespread cultivation of the closely related sugarcane and maize plants."

"Females lay 20-30 eggs within the midribs of their host-plant's leaves. Under normal conditions, development from hatchling to adult takes approximately 20 days. However, development of P. maidis nymphs is highly temperature dependent. Normal development occurs between 20-27 °C and has five juvenile instar stages. Extreme temperatures (below 10 °C and above 30 °C) result in a loss of the fifth instar and a direct molt from fourth instar to adult, but full development is extended dramatically to 74 days. Rearing at a temperature of 15 °C results in an extra, sixth, instar and a 65-day development time. P. maidis occupies warm climates and is able to reproduce year round, but development is affected by temperature changes."

"Similar to other planthoppers, two different types (morphs) of adult P. maidis can develop depending on environmental conditions. The first, brachypterous, have short, underdeveloped wings and most often develop as a response to high quality host plants, low conspecific density, and no need for dispersal. The second, macropterous, have fully developed wings and emerge when dispersal is required due to high population density or low quality host plants. The purpose of the macropters is to disperse and lay eggs on corn seedlings, whereas the brachypters are to simply feed on the growing plant and reproduce. Once the plant starts to age, more macropters are produced and the cycle continues."

There's a nice article about the lifecycle of these types of bugs by J.H. Tsai and S.W. Wilson here: https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Steve-Wilson-13/publication/233708875_Biology_of_Peregrinus_maidis_with_Descriptions_of_Immature_Stages_Homoptera_Delphacidae

Update: We later managed to make a slowed down video of the adult flapping its wings. It looks quite amazing!: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/283443073.

Where the ear and the leaf meet at the stalk part A...🔎 

As mentioned in our other main mielie 🌽 post, (https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/283369531) we're delving behind some mielie ears and sharing what we've found. 

🌍 There are whitish larva-like things that look a little bit like maggots with tiny "antennae" at both ends, as well as some peculiar brown pupae. If you look closely 🔍👀 at the pupae then you can see similar-looking white stalky bits sticking out at both ends, the ones at one end being longer than those at the other. 

It looks as if the larva-like things and the pupae are a package deal 😁 

Join us in taking an even closer look...watch as they wriggle and do their thing...the more you look, the more it seems as if the head is at the pointier side with the smaller stalky bits, and the longer stalky bits at the other end are actually "spoilers" on the rear...?

From the second video (extracted piccies 4, 5 and 6, one of them may even be munching on a buglet or excreting - there seems to be a buglet exoskeleton and quite a bit of slime! What *are* these things and what are they *doing*? Possibly some sort of fly larvae preying on the "basketball bugs" or corn planthoppers described in our other post? (https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/283414486) 

Update: We subsequently found a still-living larva right on the verge of settling down in order to pupate. It seems it decided to do so right next to another pupa, interestingly also aligned in the same direction. We had previously noticed that the pupae always seem to occur in clusters...

Looking back at all the other photos we had taken, it becomes clear that the "slanted" part of the pupa most often ends up at the "upper" end (as the mielie is positioned on the stalk), and the side with the two larger white protrusions ends up at the "lower" end. This makes sense if the protrusions are associated with the rear end of the larva which would probably rather not pupate alone, and rather with its head upward (who wouldn't, unless there are other additional issues going on? 🙂) From this we can conclude that the pupae tend to be predominantly "clustered" and "upward-facing".

Given this fact, it may pose another possible explanation. The larva in the video and three extracted piccies may well have been right on the verge of settling down in order to pupate, possibly even next to the other pupae in the photos, when we disturbed everything by peeling back the mielie leaf and picking the mielie. This could explain the semi-sedentary behaviour of this particular larva, as well as the slime. It may have been "wedged" between the leaf and the outer mielie bract, and on being disturbed, it "fell down", possibly with its lower end already attached for pupation. The bug exoskeleton, at what must be its head end, may potentially either be a last meal or a coincidence.

Looking further at the location of the living whitish larvae, it would appear that they are always located  between the mielie leaf and the outer bracts of the ear in some way. We have added two additional videos in the Facebook comments below. From them, and from our other posts about the Corn Leaf Aphids (https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/283373176) and the Corn Planthoppers (https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/283414486), this "coincidently" happens to be exactly where these insects can also be found. A coincidence? We think not! 😄 The further we go, the more it looks as if this is also some form of hoverfly larva as was found to be the case with the bright green larvae 🐛 we also found in similar locations here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/283524794.

In conclusion, given all this information, we strongly suspect that this is also a type of hoverfly larva. We'll keep an eye on some of the pupae to see what emerges...🔍👀 🤔🧐

Update: We decided to do some "maggot-rearing" to find out what emerges. Rather surprisingly it turns out that they are not hoverfly larvae at all, but they became red-eyed fruit flies! 🪰😍 We certainly didn't see that one coming - we're delighted to be surprised once again! From the research we did it looks as if the adults may possibly be "Immigrant Fruit Flies": https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/283507505.

Worming and changing...things are starting to look up in Gulu, on the outskirts of East London, Eastern Cape, South Africa 🇿🇦

#flies #fruitfly

Quoting from the original Facebook post containing additional video 🎥 footage: https://www.facebook.com/share/p/1EnedMPJyo/

The pupae have "hatched" and look what popped out, red-eyed fruit flies! 🪰😍🪰😍🪰😍🪰😍🪰😍 

Almost a month ago we harvested some mielies 🌽🌽🌽 and found a "cornucopia" of life hidden behind the ears: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/283369531. 

🌍 Among the myriad of creatures were some whitish larva-like things that looked a bit like maggots with tiny "antennae" at both ends, as well as some peculiar brown pupae clustered together: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/283499883. Their slanted ends tended to most often end up at the "upper" end (as the mielie is positioned on the stalk) and the sides with the two larger white protrusions ended up at the "lower" end. If you look closely 🔍👀 at the pupae, then you can see similar-looking white stalky bits sticking out at both ends, the ones at one end being longer than those at the other. 

At that stage we guessed that the larva-like things and the pupae were a package deal, that they were fly maggots of some form and speculated that they might become hoverflies...it seems we weren't quite on the right track! 🚉 It's a good thing we're still in training! 🚂 😊 

Curious to see what might hatch, we put one of the mielie leaves, with attached pupae, into a semi-transparent container. You could say we undertook some home "maggot-rearing" (homage, and no disrespect intended to those involved in the more "pedestrian 🦵" Caterpillar Rearing Group 🙂).The wait was on... 

As in the movies, calendar days 📆 fell to the ground like leaves from a tree 🍃...the tree started looking rather bare 🍂...and then one bright morning, there it was! A fruit fly with bright red eyes running around inside the container! 🪰😍. Not quite what we were expecting, but beautiful nonetheless! We couldn't see any holes in any of larval cases, and so, unconvinced that this was "it", we set the fruit fly free 🪰😍 and closed the lid once again. 

On the twelfth day we noticed several similar-looking red-eyed fruit flies in the container 🪰😍🪰😍🪰😍🪰😍🪰😍. Although we still couldn't see any holes in the larval cases, it was quite apparent that they somehow must have gotten out...we decided to take a closer look at the "fresh" fruit flies 🔍👀 

Looking at the photos and videos of two of the fruit flies 🪰😍🪰😍 , and comparing them to the available information online, it looks as if these fruit flies could possibly either be of the genus Scaptomyza, or of the genus Drosophila. 

If viewed from above, the heads of the Scaptomyza spp. are apparently typically "full-moon shaped" 🌕 in profile (http://www.drosophila.jp/jdd/class/030709/03070936.pdf and https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/210333-Scaptomyza). The heads of these fruit flies, however, are more "crescent-shaped" 🌒, even somewhat concave on the side closer to the body. In fact the closest match we could find seems to be the so-called "Immigrant Fruit Fly" or Drosophila immigrans: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/329845-Drosophila-immigrans. The Immigrant Fruit Flies associated with this link, however, look rather "hunchbacked". 🤔 According to these handy "ID tips for common Drosophila species" (https://www.inaturalist.org/posts/43576-id-tips-for-common-drosophila-species-not-every-fruit-fly-is-drosophila-melanogaster), however, apparently this is a gender-related feature associated with the slightly larger female ♀️ of the species. We can consequently conclude that the non-hunch-backed Immigrant Fruit Flies in our photos and videos both happen to be male ♂️. 

That still leaves the mystery of the larval cases...If all these flies had come out of the cases, why don't we see any holes? 🕳 We waited another ten days, leaving plenty of time for any remaining flies to emerge, but none did...

Let's take a closer look at those cases...🔍👀 There must surely be some form of exit...possibly a slit or some opening that can re-close after the fruit fly emerges...🤔 

We got hold of a sharp pair of tweezers and carefully prodded the empty cases...suddenly a little "trapdoor" opened and closed! Apparently the entire slanted side of the larval case transforms into a tiny hinged lid (called an "operculum"). The fruit fly must have newly opened it by pressing with its head!🚪🙂 Amazing! 

It wasn't easy to find similar-looking Drosophila spp. larval cases online, but we did manage to find some. There are similarly slanted ones together with an unhinged door here: https://www.mdpi.com/2075-4450/9/3/105 and other slanted ones here: https://phys.org/news/2013-03-mechanism-steroid-hormone-production-drosophila.html. 

So the whitish larvae are maggots, the adults may possibly be Immigrant Fruit Flies, and they hatch by pressing their way out through an operculum...But one question still remains...what do the maggots eat? 🤔 

Considering the *location* of the maggots, which seems always to have been between the mielie leaf and the outer bracts of the ear in some way, their *position* seems to have been ideal, with plenty of potential food available for the taking, right up until the day of harvest.🌽 It makes sense that the fruit fly parents would have lived, mated and laid eggs in this specific location. 

We had previously videoed one of the maggots oozing slime right next to a soft-bodied instar of a Corn Planthopper (https://www.facebook.com/share/p/3HfnxNYxKkbAJS87/?mibextid=oFDknk), so we wondered if it could possibly also be carnivorous as seems to be the case with the hoverfly larvae we also found on these mielies (https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/283524794). 

Apparently fruit fly maggots tend to feed on the surface of the decaying masses on which their eggs are laid (https://www.orkin.com/pests/flies/fruit-flies/fruit-flies-and-food). They're usually considered as herbivores and are generally reared on cornmeal (🌽!) in laboratories. It has been found, however, that under *nutritional stress conditions* very similar Drosophila melanogaster maggots can resort to eating eggs and carcasses (of insects and even other maggots). Under such conditions female fruit flies have apparently even been found to selectively oviposit on and around the carcasses of larvae of their own species (https://www.nature.com/articles/srep14285). 

So, depending on the prevailing conditions (e.g. lack of food, poor food quality or dry conditions), it's perfectly possible that the Immigrant Fruit Fly maggots may have fed on any number of things at various stages. Most maggots born earlier in the mielie season would most likely have eaten plant matter, but as the mielie plants started drying out with the onset of Autumn, it's not impossible that some maggots may also have resorted to eating eggs and carcasses, possibly including those of Corn Plant Hoppers. 

What amazing little creatures these are! 

Catching the red eyes in Gulu, on the outskirts of East London, Eastern Cape, South Africa 🇿🇦

The salad daze... 

Some time ago we found some inchy green caterpillars 🐛 on our lettuces 🥬: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/285265884 and some time later still larger ones: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/285272754. 

At that stage Suncana Bradley identified the smaller ones (similar to the smaller ones in this post) as potentially being the larvae of one of the lovely Crambid Snout Moths (Crambidae family): https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/52002-Crambidae https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6986&taxon_id=52002&view=species, and the larger ones (similar to the larger ones in this post) as little Plusiinae or Semi-Looper caterpillars, possibly the larvae of one of the Plusiine Looper Moths (Plusiinae family): https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/122455-Plusiinae and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6986&taxon_id=122455&view=species. 

We weren't quite sure about the suggestion of "rearing" them per se, since we're still trying to "rear" enough lettuce for ourselves to eat, but it seems there has apparently been some covert rearing happening in the background anyway 😅. 

Well here is another batch Suncana, we seem to have liddle biddies, teenagers and full-blown adults of different sizes all at once. Since we've already come this far, we're now curious, may we ask what these will become? The large ones seem to have black spots and something akin to a pair of wraparound sunglasses on 😎 We've decided to go ahead with the "rearing" and have isolated one of the lettuces 😁 

Update1: We subsequently reared three of the larger caterpillars with the sunglasses only to discover that they had been parasitised by Braconid Wasps 🙁 Although we were quite sad because we had grown rather fond of the caterpillars, we decided to go ahead and rear the wasps instead: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/285291566.

After our rather unconventional rearing experience we also decided to rear some of the smaller caterpillars, in the hopes that they were possibly too small to be stung by the wasps: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/285334721.

Update2: Thankfully the little caterpillars all blossomed and became beautiful Rusty Dot Pearl Moths: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/285342567. They are indeed members of the Crambid Snout Moths (Crambidae family) as suggested by Suncana! Thanks again Suncana! 🙂

Update3: Some time later we discovered another batch of caterpillars with black spots and wraparound sunglasses on our radishes (https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/288644081). We decided to rear them: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/285490498, and were delighted to discover that most of them became beautiful Scar Bank Gem or Silver U-Tail Moths here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/285497257, here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/285513280, here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/285516396 and a bonus one here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/285518534. They are indeed also members of the Plusiine Looper Moths (Plusiinae family) as Suncana had suggested. Excellent sleuthing there Suncana! Very impressive! 😄 Only one of them was sadly apparently parasitised by a Chalcidoid Wasp 😕: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/285532516.

Western Bluebird (Sialia mexicana) is a native, migratory songbird in the Thrushes (Turdidae) family that is 18cm (7 inches) long. Adult male tail, upper parts and throat are deep blue. Breast sides and flanks are chestnut colored, and belly and undertail coverts are gray. Female is duller, brownish gray above, breast and flanks tinged with chestnut, throat is pale gray. It nests in holes in trees and also in nest boxes. Bluebirds are year round residents in local (Monterey County) oak woodlands. Several nesting boxes can be seen in Toro County Park (Monterey County, CA). Diet is mostly insects and berries. It often forages by perching fairly low and flying down to the ground to capture insects, sometimes hovering briefly before pouncing. It may catch insects in mid-air or in foliage.

Breeding: "The western bluebird nests in cavities or in nest boxes, competing with tree swallows, house sparrows, and European starlings for natural nesting locations. Because of the high level of competition, house sparrows often attack western bluebirds for their nests. The attacks are made both in groups or alone. Attacks by starlings can be reduced if the nesting box opening is kept to 1.5 in (38 mm) diameter to avoid takeover. Nest boxes come into effect when the species is limited and dying out due to the following predators: cats, raccoons, opossums, and select birds of prey such as the Cooper's Hawk. Ants, bees, earwigs, and wasps can crawl into the nesting boxes and damage the newborns. Western bluebirds are among the birds that nest in cavities, or holes in trees, or nest boxes. Their beaks are too weak and small to dig out their own holes, so they rely on woodpeckers to make their nest sites for them."

description:
Quoting from the original Facebook post containing additional video 🎥 footage: https://www.facebook.com/share/p/14KGDwydH5z/

A Spider-Mite saga 😄

Just as we were sitting down to have a break in the bush, this spidey turned up.

It's clearly quite cute, but what's with the red thing? 🤔

It looks like a mite! 😮 

Simon hauled out our trusty tweezers, and tried to remove it - quite a tricky story! 😅

After a bit of a tug, it eventually dropped off, but it looks as if there may possibly be more dinky ones left...at least the worst one is off...

Edit: According to Susan Kotze this looks like a member of the Ant-Eating Spiders (Zodariidae family): https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/48893-Zodariidae, https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6986&preferred_place_id=6986&taxon_id=48893&view=species and possibly a Grass Stitcher, Chariobas sp.: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/420943-Chariobas, https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/420943-Chariobas/browse_photos and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?verifiable=true&taxon_id=420943&preferred_place_id=6986. Thanks Susan! 🙂 Interestingly, looking further on iNat, this spider looks somewhat similar to the one observed by Gigi Laidler in Soetwater, Kommetjie: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/99481093. 

"Ant spiders are members of the family Zodariidae. They are small to medium-sized eight-eyed spiders found in all tropical and subtropical regions of South America, Africa, Madagascar, Australia-New Guinea, New Zealand, Arabia and the Indian subcontinent. Most species are daytime hunters and live together with ants, mimicking their behavior and sometimes even their chemical traits. Although little is known about most zodariids, members of the genus Zodarion apparently feed only on ants; a number of other genera in the family are apparently also ant (or termite) specialists."

"Chariobas is a genus of spiders in the family Zodariidae. It was first described in 1893 by Eugène Simon. As of 2024, it contains five African species."

Apparently, according to Wessel Pretorius "These weird looking spiders make thin tube like nests between grasses, restio stalks, or bunches of leaves or foliage. They pull the stalks or leaves together and fasten them with silk." (https://www.facebook.com/groups/101951926508391/permalink/7972171682819670/?app=fbl)

Jan Botha has also helpfully pointed out that the red mites are actually True Velvet Mites (Trombidiidae family): https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/57652-Trombidiidae and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6986&preferred_place_id=6986&taxon_id=57652&view=species. Thanks Jan! 🙂

"Trombidiidae, also known as red velvet mites, true velvet mites, or rain bugs, are small arachnids (eight-legged arthropods) found in plant litter and are known for their bright red color.

While adults are typically no more than 4 mm in length, some species can grow larger and the largest, including the African Dinothrombium tinctorum and Indian Trombidium grandissimum, may exceed 12 mm. This also makes them the largest mites, if disregarding ticks engorged after feeding; unlike those, D. tinctorum and T. grandissimum are harmless to humans.

Their life pattern is in stages similar to other members of the Prostigmata: egg, pre-larva, larva, protonymph, deutonymph, tritonymph and adult (male or female). They usually have only one breeding cycle per year.

They are active predators as grown adults. As larvae they are often parasites of insects and other arachnids. This lifestyle is typical of the Parasitengona.

One well-known species from Europe, Asia, and North Africa is Trombidium holosericeum. The systematics of this group has been in flux and many former subfamilies of this are now raised to families within the Trombidioidea.

The oil from the red velvet mite Trombidium grandissimum is used in traditional Indian medicine to treat paralysis."

A moment of relief in the bush in Gulu, on the outskirts of East London, Eastern Cape, South Africa 🇿🇦

The honey-choc Lady Beetles, AKA "Somethingeus deliciosus", apparently already has a name! 😄

A few months ago, in January, we came across some rather unusual hairy little honey-choc-coloured Lady Beetles. They were pupating on a Bugweed plant: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/286740919.

We subsequently returned to see them again on the following day once their autumny colours had settled: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/286741646. 

A few days later we found another one on our Lemon 🍋 tree: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/286742671, and subsequently also on a Society Garlic Chive: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/286743766.

In the absence of an identity or name, at that stage, and inspired by the chocolatey grin on the backs of these little beetles, Jan Botha suggested "Somethingeus deliciosus" 😄🧡🤎

Since then, we've been seeing these beetles all over the place, until last week, when we came across this astonishing sight! 😮 Apparently the Somethingeous deliciosus beetles had found something even more delicious!

After one of our bush walks we happened to stroll past one of the many Yellow Bells plants in our area and we noticed that the honey-choc beetles, their eggs, larvae and pupae were all over the plant! What a surprise! 👀 We also found a pupa on a neighbouring Lantana leaf, but we are yet to establish if this is related to feeding, or purely a proximity-related coincidence...

Since we realised that Yellow Bells is categorised as invasive, we did a bit of research...

We came across this interesting fact sheet compiled by Lin Besaans for the Agricultural Research Council, "Mada Polluta, A Lady Beetle Released for Biocontrol of Yellow Bells": https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-ppri/Fact%20Sheets%20Library/Mada%20polluta%20on%20tecoma.pdf.

"The lady beetle Mada polluta Mulsant 1850 (Coleoptera: Coccinellidae) was collected on yellow bells (Tecoma stans) in 2007 in Mexico, where the plant is native, and imported into quarantine in South Africa for screening as a potential biocontrol agent. Following several years of testing, the lady beetle was found to be host specific on yellow bells. Permission was obtained for its release, and the first insects were released at various sites in KwaZulu-Natal, Mpumalanga, Gauteng, and North West in the summer of 2013/2014. Releases are on-going, and the distribution map will be updated once establishment has been determined.

Adult beetles are yellow and black, and are about 5 mm long and 4.34 mm wide. Larvae are yellow, with long, branched spines on the dorsal and lateral surfaces. From first instar to fourth instar, larval body length ranges between 2.51 mm and 5.3 mm. Pupae are yellow and brown, and are covered by the old hard, spiny skin of the larva.

Adult females lay clusters of 3-59 eggs on the underside of leaves. The larvae hatch within 7-10 days and feed on the leaves immediately. Larvae go through 4 larval instars (growth stages) before pupating, and emerge as adults within about 36 days. Adults live for up to 4 months, and females reproduce several times during that period.

Both adults and larvae feed on the leaves and, to a lesser extent, on the stems of yellow bells. They consume the leaf area in narrow, short band sets from left to right, then start again below the first set, but without ever consuming the thin line of leaf area that separates the two adjacent sets. In this manner, they skeletonise the leaf.

The lady beetle is expected to contribute significantly to the biological control of yellow bells in South Africa, owing to several factors. Firstly, both adults and larvae are extremely damaging to the plant. Laboratory studies demonstrated that the insects decrease leaf density significantly, stunting the plant’s growth and reducing its competitive ability. Secondly, adult females reproduce rapidly, thus, beetle populations and their associated damage should increase in the field accordingly. Thirdly, this group of beetles (coccinellids) protect themselves chemically from predators and parasitoids, which enhances their chance of survival and, ultimately, their effect on the target weed. Biological control is the only sustainable solution for yellow bells infestations, and it is hoped that the lady beetle will reduce these plants throughout the country, thereby encouraging the indigenous vegetation to recover."

There's another, more recent article by Marleni Arnoldi in Creamer Media's Engineering News, 19 November 2024: "ARC to release invasive-plant controlling beetles in Umkhomazi": https://m.engineeringnews.co.za/article/arc-to-release-invasive-plant-controlling-beetles-in-umkhomazi-2024-11-19, in which it is reported that:

 "The Agricultural Research Council’s (ARC’s) plant health and protection unit will, on November 25, release a leaf-feeding lady beetle called Mada Polluta in Umkhomazi, KwaZulu-Natal, to act as a biological control agent against invasive yellow bells...The release of the beetle, which is a collaboration project between the Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment, the eThekwini municipality and Ezemvelo KwaZulu-Natal Wildlife, was approved for release in 2013, and efforts are now focused on mass rearing and releasing the beetle to help control yellow bell invasions.

In particular, the release of the beetle in Umkhomazi aims to limit the growth and spread of yellow bells in the region. More releases will occur at selected sites across the province that provide suitable habitat for the beetle."

It would appear the preliminary suggestion to introduce this beetle was based on research conducted in this paper by Lulama Gracious Madire, Biocontrol Science and Technology Volume 23 (2013) - Issue 8: "Biology and host range of Mada polluta, a potential biological control agent of Tecoma stans in South Africa": https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/09583157.2013.809404.

According to another article by the same author, Lulama Gracious Madire, in Plant Protection News (October 2016 - March 2017) Issue No 109, "Lady beetle (Mada polluta) fully established on yellow bells (Tecoma stans) on the South Coast of KwaZulu-Natal": https://invasives.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/PPRI-News-109.pdf

"Since the release of this beetle, a number of factors have delayed its establishment, including the destruction of most of the release sites through deliberate felling and burning by landowners after initial establishment. Although the beetles recovered at a few felled sites,
none of the beetles were recovered on burned sites. The destruction of the release sites has not only delayed establishment of the beetle, but has also delayed the commencement of its post-release evaluation."

Well it would appear that this beetle has certainly made its way all the way to Gulu! We've since been finding them on Yellow Bells plants all over the place! 😄

From iNat we see Mada sp. Lady Beetles are Plant-Eating Lady Beetles: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/640755-Mada and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?preferred_place_id=6986&taxon_id=640755&view=species, but there 
are no observations as yet of Mada polluta on iNat despite the name apparently being listed: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/673993-Mada-polluta and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6986&taxon_id=673993&view=species. 

Update: Thanks to Tony Rebelo Mada polluta is now listed on iNat as the Yellow Bells Ladybeetle. Thanks Tony! 🙂 Thanks also to Jaroslav Větrovec* for confirming the ID 🙂

*Jaroslav Větrovec is "a Coccinellidae specialist" 

We managed to contact Lulu to send her regards from the local beetles and she kindly added that: "Indeed, Mada polluta is well established around East London. I visited East London in March, and it is causing significant damage to the Tecoma stans population. This species is specific to yellow bells; it may be found resting on the leaves of other plants when they are defoliated, but it does not feed on or develop on other plants. It is well established at South coast, KZN and Mpumalanga provinces as well." Thanks for that Lulu! 🙂

Reading up a bit further about Yellow Bells or Tecoma Stans: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/48363-Tecoma-stans and https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/48363-Tecoma-stans/browse_photos, we found the following:

"Tecoma stans is a species of flowering perennial shrub in the trumpet vine family, Bignoniaceae, that is native to the Americas. Common names include yellow trumpetbush, yellow bells, yellow elder, ginger Thomas. Tecoma stans is the official flower of the United States Virgin Islands and the floral emblem of The Bahamas.

Tecoma stans is a semi-evergreen shrub or small tree, growing up to 10 m tall. It features opposite odd-pinnate green leaves, with 3 to 13 serrate, 8- to 10-cm-long leaflets. The leaflets, glabrous on both sides, have a lanceolate blade 2–10 cm long and 1–4 cm wide, with a long acuminate apex and a wedge-shaped base.

The large, showy, golden yellow, trumpet-shaped flowers are in clusters at the ends of branches. The corolla of the flower is bell- to funnel-shaped, five-lobed (weakly two-lipped), often reddish-veined in the throat and is 3.5 to 8.5 cm long. Flowering takes place from spring to fall, but more profusely from spring to summer.

The fruits, narrow capsules, arise from two carpels and are up to 25 cm long. A fruit contains many yellow seeds with membranopus wings; when the fruit opens upon ripening, these seed are spread by the wind (anemochory). The flowers attract bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds. Apart from sexually by seed, Tecoma stans can also be reproduced asexually by stem cuttings. 

Tecoma stans is native to the Americas. It extends from the southern United States through Mexico, Central America, and the Antilles to northern Venezuela, and through the Andes mountain range to northern Argentina. It was introduced in southern Africa, India, and Hawaii. It is evergreen in moist and warmer regions, but is deciduous in more temperate regions that have a pronounced dry season.

Yellow trumpetbush is a ruderal species, readily colonizing disturbed, rocky, sandy, and cleared land and occasionally becoming an invasive weed. It thrives in a wide variety of ecosystems, from high altitude temperate forests and tropical deciduous and evergreen forests, to xerophilous scrub and the intertropical littoral. It quickly colonizes disturbed, rocky, sandy, and cleared fields. The species prefers dry and sunny regions of the coast. 

Tecoma stans is drought-tolerant and grows well in warm climates. It is cultivated as an ornamental. They are grown in many parts of the world for their beautiful flowering, to adorn streets and gardens. It can be easily propagated by stem cuttings.

The wood of Tecoma stans is used in rustic architecture like bahareque, for the construction of furniture and canoes, or as firewood or charcoal. It is a medicinal plant used against diabetes and against diseases of the digestive system, among other uses. The plant is desirable fodder when it grows in fields grazed by livestock.

It is a very potent anti-venom against cobra venom, used by Pakistani old medicine. It is proved to be better than antiserum, the paste of this plant's leaves are applied topically on the cobra bite. Its bio-chemicals bind with the cobra venom enzymes thus effectively inhibiting the venom.

Tecoma stans is unique in that although it is nontoxic itself, the honey from its flowers is poisonous nonetheless.

Tecoma stans has invasive potential and occasionally becomes a weed. The species is considered invasive in Africa (especially South Africa), South America, Asia, Australia and the Pacific Islands. It now presents a significant danger for biodiversity. It competes with local species and can form thick, almost monospecific thickets."

Quoting from the original Facebook post containing additional video 🎥 footage: https://www.facebook.com/share/p/1YXsju8PZT/

Oh...this isn't what we expected...

A little while ago we came across some peculiar inchy green caterpillars 🐛🐛🐛 with something akin to wraparound sunglasses on our lettuces 🥬 and we decided to rear them to find out what they would become: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/285277062.

After feeding them for several days we became rather attached to the caterpillars and were quite excited to see them fattening up, slowing down and getting ready to pupate 😃 Following up on their appearance and matching it to other caterpillars we found online, we expected that they could possibly become something like Ctenoplusia sp. moths: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6986&taxon_id=174099&view=species or Silver Y, Autographa gamma moths: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/55651-Autographa-gamma/browse_photos.

Boy oh boy were we heartbroken 💔😔 to see what happened next! It turns out that each and every one of the three caterpillars we kept had been parasitised...

One after the other we found them thrashing about, covered in grey marks (piccy one) where the parisitic larvae had presumably emerged. Piccy two is one of the larvae that must have become detached from the caterpillar before it could spin a cocoon on top of it together with all its siblings. It's spinning a solitary home...

The rest of larvae seem to have formed a cocoon housing complex on top of the caterpillar which subsequently dropped out leaving the cluster behind (piccy 3). These cocoons looked rather familiar to us, like ones we had previously discovered elsewhere in the garden: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/285303943.

Although we were rather disappointed, we decided to find out what kind of parisitoid this was. We kept the cocoons and waited to see what would happen...

After 12 days we suddenly noticed a mass of tiny wasps had emerged (sampled video piccy 4). There were well over 50 tiny wasps coming out of the first cocoon cluster alone!

From the remaining sampled video piccies, you can see how the newborns clean themselves (those looong antennae! and tiny back leggies 😄), and run around. Their bodies are about 2.5mm long excluding wings and antennae. It looks as if they use their incredibly long antennae to "tap", "tap" around, sensing and feeling their new environment as they go. What a remarkable sight!

If you look carefully at the piccies the cocoon clusters you can see tiny opens lids where the wasplets must have emerged.

Edit: According to Alan Manson, these are in fact members of the Braconid Wasps (Braconidae family): https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/244423-Microgastrinae#cite_note-1, and more specifically belonging to the Microgastrinae subfamily: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/244423-Microgastrinae and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6986&preferred_place_id=6986&taxon_id=244423&view=species. Thanks for the help Alan! 🙂 Thanks for confirming the ID Annari du Plessis and Suncana Bradley 🙂

"The Braconidae are a family of parasitoid wasps. After the closely related Ichneumonidae, braconids make up the second-largest family in the order Hymenoptera, with about 17,000 recognized species and many thousands more undescribed. One analysis estimated a total between 30,000 and 50,000, and another provided a narrower estimate between 42,000 and 43,000 species...

The larvae of most braconids are internal or external primary parasitoids of other insects, especially the larval stages of Coleoptera, Diptera, and Lepidoptera, but also some hemimetabolous insects such as aphids, Heteroptera, or Embiidina. Most species kill their hosts, though some cause the hosts to become sterile and less active. Parasitoidy on adult insects (particularly on Hemiptera and Coleoptera) also occurs. Members of two subfamilies, the Mesostoinae and Doryctinae are known to form galls on plants. Braconids are often used as biological pest control agents, especially against aphids...

Endoparasitoid species often display elaborate physiological adaptations to enhance larval survival within the host, such as the co-option of endosymbiotic viruses for compromising host immune defenses. These bracoviruses are often used by the wasps instead of, or in addition to, a venom cocktail. The DNA of the wasp actually contains portions that are the templates for the components of the viral particles and they are assembled in an organ in the female's abdomen known as the calyx."

"Microgastrinae is a subfamily of braconid wasps, encompassing almost 3,000 described species, with an estimated 30,000–50,000 total species. This makes it one of the richest subfamilies with the most species of parasitoid wasps...

These wasps are small, with 18 segmented antennae. Most species are black or brown, a few are more colorful. Many species are morphologically similar enough to be considered cryptic species. Species within this subfamily have a worldwide distribution. 135 species of Microgastrinae have been confirmed from Canada, though the number may be as high as 275. At least 28 species have been identified from Turkey in Gökçeada and Bozcaada.

Microgastrinae are koinobiont, primary endoparasitoids of larval Lepidoptera. While most species are solitary, many are gregarious, meaning multiple wasp eggs develop within the same caterpillar. When the eggs hatch the wasp larvae feed on the hemolymph and organs of their host. Once fully developed, the larvae exit the dying caterpillar and immediately spin silken cocoons where they pupate.

Microgastrinae is one of six subfamilies of Braconidae which carry polydnaviruses.

More than 100 species of Microgastrinae have been used in biological control programs.

Microgastrinae need the virus to be able to reproduce. How it is exactly done is by injecting eggs with the proviral genome plus virions into the host's cavity. The virions then infect and discharge their DNA into the host's cells, stopping it from killing the wasp's offspring and instead promoting its growth inside the host's body."

Update: Some time later we discovered another batch of caterpillars with black spots and wraparound sunglasses on our radishes. We decided to rear them and were delighted to discover that they became beautiful Scar Bank Gem or Silver U-Tail moths 😃: https://www.facebook.com/share/p/D9dzDdu4zjTPnkFX/?mibextid=oFDknk.

Sad about the old, but welcoming the new in Gulu, on the outskirts of East London, Eastern Cape, South Africa 🇿🇦
