Quoting from the original Facebook post containing additional video 🎥 footage: https://www.facebook.com/share/p/1FWfRSfsy5/

Masses if tiiiiiiny parasitising wasps! 😯

A while ago we found a set of caterpillars that look as if they're wearing wraparound sunglasses 😎🐛 on our radishes and we decided to try to rear them: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/285490498

Most of the caterpillars, four in all, became stunning Scar Bank Gem or Silver U-Tail Moths, Ctenoplusia limbirena 😃 here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/285497257, here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/285513280, here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/285516396 and here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/285518534.

We were a little puzzled to find one seemingly anomalous caterpillar that had decided to cocoon on a lettuce leaf. The other caterpillars tended to climb up to a high point and spin a cocoon on the side of a fixed surface such as the container lid or edge. Due to the peculiar behaviour we observed, we were at first not sure whether this was indeed a wraparound sunglass caterpillar to begin with, since we were also rearing other types of caterpillars, Leaf-Roller caterpillars, at the same time. In retrospect it looks as if this must indeed have been a wraparound sunglass caterpillar, since the amount of cocoon silk is very typical of these caterpillars, and not of the Leaf-Roller caterpillars. The peculiar behaviour of the caterpillar may also be due to what we discovered next...

After about 13 days from cocooning, this happened! Sadly it seems the caterpillar must already have been stung by a parasitising wasp even before we started rearing it! 🙁

Apparently it's quite well-known that parasiting wasps can even affect the conduct of their hosts to the extent that they may even end up protecting and defending their parasites. See for example https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parasitoid_wasp and an article by Matt Simon: "Absurd Creature of the Week: The Wasp That Lays Eggs Inside Caterpillars and Turns Them Into Slaves": https://www.wired.com/2014/10/absurd-creature-week-glyptapanteles-wasp-caterpillar-bodyguard/. It would appear that the caterpillar was already quite affected in its conduct prior to cocooning...

We had previously tried to rear some similar-looking caterpillars which we had found on our lettuces, but we were subsequently disappointed to find that every single one of those caterpillars had been parasitised by Braconid Wasps which we then decided to rear: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/285291566.

In that case there were in the region of about 50 parasitic wasps emerging from each of the cocoon clusters associated with each of the caterpillars. In each case there was still a considerable proportion of the caterpillar body remaining. The bodies of the wasps were quite large, around 2.5mm long excluding wings and antennae. The antennae of the wasps were quite long compared to their body lengths.

The wasps associated with this caterpillar, however, are quite different. There are roughly a thousand tiny wasps which have emerged from just this one caterpillar! There are no tiny wasp cocoons in evidence, and the caterpillar body has been completely consumed. The bodies of these wasps are about 3/4mm long excluding wings and antennae, and the antennae are quite short compared to their body lengths.

It seems these two wasp-caterpillar parisitisations and parasitoids are certainly quite different!

Edit1: According to Johan Heyns these might possibly be Chalcid wasps (Chalcidoidea superfamily): https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/69750-Chalcidoidea and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6986&preferred_place_id=6986&taxon_id=69750&view=species. Thanks Johan! 🙂 Thanks also for  confirming the ID for us Suncana! 🙂

"Chalcid wasps (/ˈkælsɪd/, from Greek khalkos 'copper', for their metallic colour) are insects within the superfamily Chalcidoidea, part of the order Hymenoptera. The superfamily contains some 22,500 known species, and an estimated total diversity of more than 500,000 species, meaning the vast majority have yet to be discovered and described. The name "chalcid" is often confused with the name "chalcidid", though the latter refers strictly to one constituent family, the Chalcididae, rather than the superfamily as a whole; accordingly, most recent publications use the name "chalcidoid" when referring to members of the superfamily.

Most chalcid wasps are parasitoids of other insects, though other life styles are known, with the herbivorous fig wasps acting as pollinators. Various species are used as biological pest control agents or in scientific research.

Chalcidoids are generally small wasps, averaging 1.5 mm in length and usually being less than 3 mm. The body is often metallic in colour. The wings may be developed, reduced or absent. When the wings are developed, they have reduced venation or sometimes none at all.

However, the group is morphologically very diverse. Chalcidoids range in size from up to 41.7 mm long...

Most chalcidoids are parasitoids, their hosts including insects, spiders, ticks and mites, pseudoscorpions and even gall-forming nematodes. Some species parasitise a wide range of hosts, while others have a narrow host range. They attack host life stages ranging from eggs to adults. The superfamily includes primary, secondary and tertiary parasitoids, both ecto- and endoparasitoids, and both solitary and gregarious parasitoids.

There are also herbivorous chalcidoids within the families of Agaonidae, Epichrysomallidae, Eurytomidae, Eulophidae, Melanosomellidae, Ormyridae, Pteromalidae, Tanaostigmatidae and Torymidae. Agaonidae only develop within figs...

Chalcidoidea is one of the most important taxa of biological control agents. They are used to control pest insects in both natural and agricultural ecosystems. Some herbivorous species are also used in biological control, such as the melanosomellid Trichilogaster acaciaelongifoliae for control of the weed Acacia longifolia.

There are also chalcidoids that are agricultural pests themselves, mainly attacking plant seeds. Bruchophagus attack seeds of legumes (e.g. alfalfa), Systole attack seeds of Apiaceae used as spices (e.g. coriander) and Megastigmus attack seeds of Pinaceae grown in plantations.

Females of family Agaonidae are important as pollinators of figs.

Some chalcidoids, especially those in genera Trichogramma (Trichogrammatidae) and Nasonia (Pteromalidae) are model organisms in scientific research. They have been used to study sex determination, the influence of bacterial endosymbionts and the genetics of speciation. The genome of moth parasitoid Copidosoma floridanum was sequenced as part of the i5K project."

Edit2: According to Mark G Wright these wasps may possibly even be Copidosoma sp. famous for polyembreony: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/250287-Copidosoma and https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/250287-Copidosoma/browse_photos. That's really interesting Mark, thanks so much! 🙂

"Copidosoma is a genus of chalcid wasps, which are parasitoids of Lepidoptera. The wasps are polyembryonic, depositing one or two eggs into their host which then develop into multiple offspring and have a soldier caste and a reproductive caste...

They are mainly polyembryonic parasitoids of the caterpillars of Lepidoptera and have been deliberately introduced into many areas as biological control agents for agricultural pests, e.g. Copidosoma floridanum was introduced to Hawaii to control the tomato looper (Chrysodeixis chalcites) while Copidosoma koehleri is used extensively in control of the potato tuber moth (Phthorimaea operculella) and Copidosoma primulum has been used in China to control the cotton bollworm (Helicoverpa armigera) in wheat crops.

"The wasps of the genus Copidosoma are also of interest because they are polyembryonic, i.e. more than one embryo can be found in a single egg, and they have developed a caste system where an embryo can develop into a reproductive adult or a soldier caste. The wasp lays its egg into the host moth's egg and after the caterpillar hatches it undergoes a number of instar stages until it reaches its final instar and during this time the wasp's egg produces as many as 3000 embryos through cloning, these form an assemblage called a polymorula and live as endoparasitoids in the host.

In a study on C. floridanum 24% of the members in the polymorula, of either sex, develop in to soldiers and when the host is killed in its final instar these soldiers die too while their siblings consume the host and pupate to emerge as adults around two weeks later. Like other Hymenoptera the females are produced from fertilised eggs and the males from unfertilised eggs, female eggs produce a higher number of soldiers throughout development while male eggs produce fewer and only in the later stages of the cycle. Where there is more than one brood, where more than one egg has been laid in a host the soldier caste from the first female brood will kill all any larvae from subsequent eggs laid, except that if a male brood is older and from a different mother then the females will co-exist with the males. It appears that the early emerging female soldiers purpose is inter-specific competition, they ensure that the first female brood has the host to themselves by killing other non related and females and related and younger males, while the later soldiers are produced to defend the host from intra-specific competitors and are produced by both sexes, although male soldiers of C. floridanum lack aggression and their production may be a trait which is being selected against.

Most species of this genus are quite host specific and use a few species of moth as their hosts and phylogenetic analysis indicates that the more closely related the species of wasp are to one another the more similar the species of host selected tend to be. For example the wasps of the species group named after Copidosoma cervius are all parasitoids of moths in the family Geometridae while those in the nacoliae species group attack caterpillars of the families Pyralidae and Tortricidae."

Wow - that is completely astonishing! So these tiny wasps already parasitise the egg laid by the moth and proceed to control the emerging caterpillar from birth until it cocoons...as we surmised, "It would appear that the caterpillar was already quite affected in its conduct prior to cocooning."

We subsequently came across a really interesting article describing how the death of the male wasp soldiers/larvae mentioned, can be viewed as self-sacrifice of the males in preference for their sibling clones (brothers) which ultimately ensures the survival of all. There are some really helpful illustrations which make it easier to visualise what's possibly going on inside these caterpillars. Anystis mites have red bodies, the adults are approximately 3 mm in length and they move in a circular motion (they are sometimes called whirligig mites for this reason!).

©️ This is a duplicate of the Yellow Bells Ladybeetle post (part B of a 2 part observation) here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/286746475.

The honey-choc Lady Beetles, AKA "Somethingeus deliciosus", apparently already has a name! 😄

A few months ago, in January, we came across some rather unusual hairy little honey-choc-coloured Lady Beetles. They were pupating on a Bugweed plant: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/286740919.

We subsequently returned to see them again on the following day once their autumny colours had settled: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/286741646. 

A few days later we found another one on our Lemon 🍋 tree: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/286742671, and subsequently also on a Society Garlic Chive: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/286743766.

In the absence of an identity or name, at that stage, and inspired by the chocolatey grin on the backs of these little beetles, Jan Botha suggested "Somethingeus deliciosus" 😄🧡🤎

Since then, we've been seeing these beetles all over the place, until last week, when we came across this astonishing sight! 😮 Apparently the Somethingeous deliciosus beetles had found something even more delicious!

After one of our bush walks we happened to stroll past one of the many Yellow Bells plants in our area and we noticed that the honey-choc beetles, their eggs, larvae and pupae were all over the plant! What a surprise! 👀 We also found a pupa on a neighbouring Lantana leaf, but we are yet to establish if this is related to feeding, or purely a proximity-related coincidence...

Since we realised that Yellow Bells is categorised as invasive, we did a bit of research...

We came across this interesting fact sheet compiled by Lin Besaans for the Agricultural Research Council, "Mada Polluta, A Lady Beetle Released for Biocontrol of Yellow Bells": https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-ppri/Fact%20Sheets%20Library/Mada%20polluta%20on%20tecoma.pdf.

"The lady beetle Mada polluta Mulsant 1850 (Coleoptera: Coccinellidae) was collected on yellow bells (Tecoma stans) in 2007 in Mexico, where the plant is native, and imported into quarantine in South Africa for screening as a potential biocontrol agent. Following several years of testing, the lady beetle was found to be host specific on yellow bells. Permission was obtained for its release, and the first insects were released at various sites in KwaZulu-Natal, Mpumalanga, Gauteng, and North West in the summer of 2013/2014. Releases are on-going, and the distribution map will be updated once establishment has been determined.

Adult beetles are yellow and black, and are about 5 mm long and 4.34 mm wide. Larvae are yellow, with long, branched spines on the dorsal and lateral surfaces. From first instar to fourth instar, larval body length ranges between 2.51 mm and 5.3 mm. Pupae are yellow and brown, and are covered by the old hard, spiny skin of the larva.

Adult females lay clusters of 3-59 eggs on the underside of leaves. The larvae hatch within 7-10 days and feed on the leaves immediately. Larvae go through 4 larval instars (growth stages) before pupating, and emerge as adults within about 36 days. Adults live for up to 4 months, and females reproduce several times during that period.

Both adults and larvae feed on the leaves and, to a lesser extent, on the stems of yellow bells. They consume the leaf area in narrow, short band sets from left to right, then start again below the first set, but without ever consuming the thin line of leaf area that separates the two adjacent sets. In this manner, they skeletonise the leaf.

The lady beetle is expected to contribute significantly to the biological control of yellow bells in South Africa, owing to several factors. Firstly, both adults and larvae are extremely damaging to the plant. Laboratory studies demonstrated that the insects decrease leaf density significantly, stunting the plant’s growth and reducing its competitive ability. Secondly, adult females reproduce rapidly, thus, beetle populations and their associated damage should increase in the field accordingly. Thirdly, this group of beetles (coccinellids) protect themselves chemically from predators and parasitoids, which enhances their chance of survival and, ultimately, their effect on the target weed. Biological control is the only sustainable solution for yellow bells infestations, and it is hoped that the lady beetle will reduce these plants throughout the country, thereby encouraging the indigenous vegetation to recover."

There's another, more recent article by Marleni Arnoldi in Creamer Media's Engineering News, 19 November 2024: "ARC to release invasive-plant controlling beetles in Umkhomazi": https://m.engineeringnews.co.za/article/arc-to-release-invasive-plant-controlling-beetles-in-umkhomazi-2024-11-19, in which it is reported that:

 "The Agricultural Research Council’s (ARC’s) plant health and protection unit will, on November 25, release a leaf-feeding lady beetle called Mada Polluta in Umkhomazi, KwaZulu-Natal, to act as a biological control agent against invasive yellow bells...The release of the beetle, which is a collaboration project between the Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment, the eThekwini municipality and Ezemvelo KwaZulu-Natal Wildlife, was approved for release in 2013, and efforts are now focused on mass rearing and releasing the beetle to help control yellow bell invasions.

In particular, the release of the beetle in Umkhomazi aims to limit the growth and spread of yellow bells in the region. More releases will occur at selected sites across the province that provide suitable habitat for the beetle."

It would appear the preliminary suggestion to introduce this beetle was based on research conducted in this paper by Lulama Gracious Madire, Biocontrol Science and Technology Volume 23 (2013) - Issue 8: "Biology and host range of Mada polluta, a potential biological control agent of Tecoma stans in South Africa": https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/09583157.2013.809404.

According to another article by the same author, Lulama Gracious Madire, in Plant Protection News (October 2016 - March 2017) Issue No 109, "Lady beetle (Mada polluta) fully established on yellow bells (Tecoma stans) on the South Coast of KwaZulu-Natal": https://invasives.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/PPRI-News-109.pdf

"Since the release of this beetle, a number of factors have delayed its establishment, including the destruction of most of the release sites through deliberate felling and burning by landowners after initial establishment. Although the beetles recovered at a few felled sites,
none of the beetles were recovered on burned sites. The destruction of the release sites has not only delayed establishment of the beetle, but has also delayed the commencement of its post-release evaluation."

Well it would appear that this beetle has certainly made its way all the way to Gulu! We've since been finding them on Yellow Bells plants all over the place! 😄

From iNat we see Mada sp. Lady Beetles are Plant-Eating Lady Beetles: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/640755-Mada and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?preferred_place_id=6986&taxon_id=640755&view=species, but there no observations as yet of Mada polluta on iNat despite the name apparently being listed: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/673993-Mada-polluta and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6986&taxon_id=673993&view=species. 

Update: Thanks to the Tony Rebelo  the Mada polluta is now listed on iNat as the Yellow Bells Ladybeetle. Thanks Tony! 🙂

We managed to contact Lulu to send her regards from the local beetles and she kindly added that: "Indeed, Mada polluta is well established around East London. I visited East London in March, and it is causing significant damage to the Tecoma stans population. This species is specific to yellow bells; it may be found resting on the leaves of other plants when they are defoliated, but it does not feed on or develop on other plants. It is well established at South coast, KZN and Mpumalanga provinces as well." Thanks for that Lulu! 🙂

Reading up a bit further about Yellow Bells or Tecoma Stans: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/48363-Tecoma-stans and https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/48363-Tecoma-stans/browse_photos, we found the following:

"Tecoma stans is a species of flowering perennial shrub in the trumpet vine family, Bignoniaceae, that is native to the Americas. Common names include yellow trumpetbush, yellow bells, yellow elder, ginger Thomas. Tecoma stans is the official flower of the United States Virgin Islands and the floral emblem of The Bahamas.

Tecoma stans is a semi-evergreen shrub or small tree, growing up to 10 m tall. It features opposite odd-pinnate green leaves, with 3 to 13 serrate, 8- to 10-cm-long leaflets. The leaflets, glabrous on both sides, have a lanceolate blade 2–10 cm long and 1–4 cm wide, with a long acuminate apex and a wedge-shaped base.

The large, showy, golden yellow, trumpet-shaped flowers are in clusters at the ends of branches. The corolla of the flower is bell- to funnel-shaped, five-lobed (weakly two-lipped), often reddish-veined in the throat and is 3.5 to 8.5 cm long. Flowering takes place from spring to fall, but more profusely from spring to summer.

The fruits, narrow capsules, arise from two carpels and are up to 25 cm long. A fruit contains many yellow seeds with membranopus wings; when the fruit opens upon ripening, these seed are spread by the wind (anemochory). The flowers attract bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds. Apart from sexually by seed, Tecoma stans can also be reproduced asexually by stem cuttings. 

Tecoma stans is native to the Americas. It extends from the southern United States through Mexico, Central America, and the Antilles to northern Venezuela, and through the Andes mountain range to northern Argentina. It was introduced in southern Africa, India, and Hawaii. It is evergreen in moist and warmer regions, but is deciduous in more temperate regions that have a pronounced dry season.

Yellow trumpetbush is a ruderal species, readily colonizing disturbed, rocky, sandy, and cleared land and occasionally becoming an invasive weed. It thrives in a wide variety of ecosystems, from high altitude temperate forests and tropical deciduous and evergreen forests, to xerophilous scrub and the intertropical littoral. It quickly colonizes disturbed, rocky, sandy, and cleared fields. The species prefers dry and sunny regions of the coast. 

Tecoma stans is drought-tolerant and grows well in warm climates. It is cultivated as an ornamental. They are grown in many parts of the world for their beautiful flowering, to adorn streets and gardens. It can be easily propagated by stem cuttings.

The wood of Tecoma stans is used in rustic architecture like bahareque, for the construction of furniture and canoes, or as firewood or charcoal. It is a medicinal plant used against diabetes and against diseases of the digestive system, among other uses. The plant is desirable fodder when it grows in fields grazed by livestock.

It is a very potent anti-venom against cobra venom, used by Pakistani old medicine. It is proved to be better than antiserum, the paste of this plant's leaves are applied topically on the cobra bite. Its bio-chemicals bind with the cobra venom enzymes thus effectively inhibiting the venom.

Tecoma stans is unique in that although it is nontoxic itself, the honey from its flowers is poisonous nonetheless.

Tecoma stans has invasive potential and occasionally becomes a weed. The species is considered invasive in Africa (especially South Africa), South America, Asia, Australia and the Pacific Islands. It now presents a significant danger for biodiversity. It competes with local species and can form thick, almost monospecific thickets."

A Spider-Mite saga 😄

Just as we were sitting down to have a break in the bush, this spidey turned up.

It's clearly quite cute, but what's with the red thing? 🤔

It looks like a mite! 😮

Simon hauled out our trusty tweezers, and tried to remove it - quite a tricky story! 😅

After a bit of a tug, it eventually dropped off, but it looks as if there may possibly be more dinky ones left...at least the worst one is off...

Edit: According to Susan Kotze this looks like a member of the Ant-Eating Spiders (Zodariidae family): https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/48893-Zodariidae, https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6986&preferred_place_id=6986&taxon_id=48893&view=species and possibly a Grass Stitcher, Chariobas sp.: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/420943-Chariobas, https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/420943-Chariobas/browse_photos and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?verifiable=true&taxon_id=420943&preferred_place_id=6986. Thanks Susan! 🙂 Interestingly, looking further on iNat, this spider looks somewhat similar to the one observed by Gigi Laidler in Soetwater, Kommetjie: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/99481093.

"Ant spiders are members of the family Zodariidae. They are small to medium-sized eight-eyed spiders found in all tropical and subtropical regions of South America, Africa, Madagascar, Australia-New Guinea, New Zealand, Arabia and the Indian subcontinent. Most species are daytime hunters and live together with ants, mimicking their behavior and sometimes even their chemical traits. Although little is known about most zodariids, members of the genus Zodarion apparently feed only on ants; a number of other genera in the family are apparently also ant (or termite) specialists."

"Chariobas is a genus of spiders in the family Zodariidae. It was first described in 1893 by Eugène Simon. As of 2024, it contains five African species."

Apparently, according to Wessel Pretorius "These weird looking spiders make thin tube like nests between grasses, restio stalks, or bunches of leaves or foliage. They pull the stalks or leaves together and fasten them with silk." (https://www.facebook.com/groups/101951926508391/permalink/7972171682819670/?app=fbl)

Jan Botha has also helpfully pointed out that the red mites are actually True Velvet Mites (Trombidiidae family): https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/57652-Trombidiidae and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6986&preferred_place_id=6986&taxon_id=57652&view=species. Thanks Jan! 🙂

"Trombidiidae, also known as red velvet mites, true velvet mites, or rain bugs, are small arachnids (eight-legged arthropods) found in plant litter and are known for their bright red color.

While adults are typically no more than 4 mm in length, some species can grow larger and the largest, including the African Dinothrombium tinctorum and Indian Trombidium grandissimum, may exceed 12 mm. This also makes them the largest mites, if disregarding ticks engorged after feeding; unlike those, D. tinctorum and T. grandissimum are harmless to humans.

Their life pattern is in stages similar to other members of the Prostigmata: egg, pre-larva, larva, protonymph, deutonymph, tritonymph and adult (male or female). They usually have only one breeding cycle per year.

They are active predators as grown adults. As larvae they are often parasites of insects and other arachnids. This lifestyle is typical of the Parasitengona.

One well-known species from Europe, Asia, and North Africa is Trombidium holosericeum. The systematics of this group has been in flux and many former subfamilies of this are now raised to families within the Trombidioidea.

The oil from the red velvet mite Trombidium grandissimum is used in traditional Indian medicine to treat paralysis."

This plant is possibly a Lettuce, Lactuca sativa: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/122976-Lactuca-sativa and https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/122976-Lactuca-sativa/browse_photos.

"Lettuce (Lactuca sativa) is an annual plant of the family Asteraceae mostly grown as a leaf vegetable. The leaves are most often used raw in green salads, although lettuce is also seen in other kinds of food, such as sandwiches, wraps and soups; it can also be grilled. Its stem and seeds are sometimes used; celtuce (asparagus lettuce) is one variety grown for its stems, which are eaten either raw or cooked. In addition to its main use as a leafy green, it has also gathered religious and medicinal significance over centuries of human consumption. Europe and North America originally dominated the market for lettuce, but by the late 20th century the consumption of lettuce had spread throughout the world. In 2023, world production of lettuce (and chicory) was 28 million tonnes, led by China with 53% of the total.

Lettuce was originally farmed by the ancient Egyptians, who transformed it from a plant whose seeds were used to obtain oil into an important food crop raised for its succulent leaves and oil-rich seeds. Lettuce spread to the Greeks and Romans; the latter gave it the name lactuca, from which the English lettuce is derived. By 50 AD, many types were described, and lettuce appeared often in medieval writings, including several herbals. The 16th through 18th centuries saw the development of many varieties in Europe, and by the mid-18th century, cultivars were described that can still be found in modern gardens.

Generally grown as a hardy annual, lettuce is easily cultivated, although it requires relatively low temperatures to prevent it from flowering quickly. It can be plagued by numerous nutrient deficiencies, as well as insect and mammal pests, and fungal and bacterial diseases. L. sativa crosses easily within the species and with some other species within the genus Lactuca. Although this trait can be a problem to home gardeners who attempt to save seeds, biologists have used it to broaden the gene pool of cultivated lettuce varieties.

Contaminated lettuce is often a source of bacterial, viral, and parasitic outbreaks in humans, including E. coli and Salmonella.

Lactuca sativa is a member of the Lactuca (lettuce) genus and the Asteraceae (sunflower or aster) family. The species was first described in 1753 by Carl Linnaeus in the second volume of his Species Plantarum. Synonyms for L. sativa include Lactuca scariola var. sativa, L. scariola var. integrata and L. scariola var. integrifolia. L. scariola is itself a synonym for L. serriola, the common wild or prickly lettuce. L. sativa also has many identified taxonomic groups, subspecies and varieties, which delineate the various cultivar groups of domesticated lettuce. Lettuce is closely related to several Lactuca species from southwest Asia; the closest relationship is to L. serriola, an aggressive weed common in temperate and subtropical zones in much of the world.

The Romans referred to lettuce as lactuca (lac meaning "milk" in Latin), an allusion to the white substance, latex, exuded by cut stems. The name Lactuca has become the genus name, while sativa (meaning "sown" or "cultivated") was added to create the species name. The current word lettuce, originally from Middle English, came from the Old French letues or laitues, which derived from the Roman name. The name romaine came from the variety of lettuce grown in the Roman papal gardens, while cos, another term for romaine lettuce, came from the earliest European seeds of the type from the Greek island of Kos, a center of lettuce farming in the Byzantine period."

Wow! We weren't expecting this! 😮

We've often seen these tiny metallic green flies here in Gulu, but this is the first time we've seen one apparently eating another teeny winged insect! Who would have known?

The green fly is a Long-Legged Fly, Dolichopodidae sp.: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/68020-Dolichopodidae, and possibly a member of the Chrysosomatini tribe: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6986&subview=map&taxon_id=1309119&view=species and: https://www.facebook.com/groups/Butterfliesandbugs/permalink/6966382546792519/?app=fbl.

"Dolichopodidae, the long-legged flies, are a large, cosmopolitan family of true flies with more than 8,000 described species in about 250 genera. The genus Dolichopus is the most speciose, with some 600 species.

Dolichopodidae generally are small flies with large, prominent eyes and a metallic cast to their appearance, though there is considerable variation among the species. Most have long legs, though some do not. In many species, the males have unusually large genitalia which are taxonomically useful in identifying species. Most adults are predatory on other small animals, though some may scavenge or act as kleptoparasites of spiders or other predators.

Dolichopodidae are a family of flies ranging in size from minute to medium-sized (1 mm to 9 mm). They have characteristically long and slender legs, though their leg length is not as striking as in families such as the Tipulidae. Their posture often is stilt-like standing high on their legs, with the body almost erect. In colour most species have a green-to-blue metallic lustre, but various other species are dull yellow, brown or black...

In most species the mouthparts are short and have a wide aperture as an adaptation for sucking small prey...

Adults of the Dolichopodidae live largely in grassy places and shrubbery. The flies occur in a wide range of habitats, near water or in meadows, woodland edges and in gardens. Some groups are confined to wet places including sands on the banks of water bodies; examples include genera such as Porphyrops, Tachytrechus, Campsicnemus, and Teuchophorus. No truly aquatic species have been described, but many are semi-aquatic and live in or near water margins. A small number of species develop on the shores of saline inland bodies of water or the intertidal zone of seashores. An example of a species that develop close to water is P. nobilitatus, they can be found congregating around lakes and ponds. Other groups are found on trunks of trees damaged by bark beetles. Adults often are seen in a characteristic predatory posture standing high on their legs on the ground or on vegetation, tree trunks or rocks, and some species walk about on the surface of still water.

The adults are predators, feeding on small invertebrates including Collembola, aphids, and the larvae of Oligochaeta. Species of the genus Dolichopus commonly prey on the larvae of mosquitoes.

The larvae occupy a wide range of habitats. Many are predators of small invertebrates and generally live in moist environments such as soil, moist sand, or rotting organic matter. Genera such as Medetera live as predators under tree bark or in the tunnels of bark beetles. Larvae of the genus Thrypticus are unusual among Dolichopodidae, in that they are phytophagous and live in the stems of reeds and other monocots near water.

Many studies have shown that Dolichopodidae give visual, rather than chemical or other signals during courtship. The males of many species exhibit elaborate secondary sexual characters assumed to aid in species recognition during courtship. These characters include flaglike flattening of the arista and tarsi, strongly modified setae and projections of the tarsi, the prolongation and deformation of podomeres, orientated silvery pruinosity, and maculation or modification of the wings."

Interestingly Jan Botha commented that he "Saw dolly 1st time in apple orchard feeding on mites (ERM) around 1988, Grabouw." Thanks for sharing about that Jan 🙂

We looked up ERM is and learned a bit more about them from an article by Jim Walgenbach, Extension Entomology Specialist (Fruits/Vegetables) Entomology, "European Red Mite": https://content.ces.ncsu.edu/european-red-mite-1

"European red mite (Panonychus ulmi; ERM) is found on fruit trees, shade trees, and shrubs worldwide. It is the most common mite occurring on apple trees...

ERM feed on leaves. When populations are severe, leaves may lose color or become brown (a condition referred to as "bronzing"). This can lead to fewer fruit, dropped fruit, and lower fruit quality, as well as a lower return bloom the following season.

Many factors determine the severity of a mite infestation, including the time of year when injury occurs, the duration of feeding, the trees' vigor and cultivar, crop load, and weather conditions."

There's another interesting article by Ricky E. Foster, Extension Entomologist, "Fruit Insects EUROPEAN RED MITE MANAGEMENT": https://extension.entm.purdue.edu/publications/E-258/E-258.html

"Prior to the advent of modern, synthetic insecticides, European red mites (ERM) were not considered a significant pest of tree fruits. ERM are what entomologists call a “secondary pest,” which means that they generally only became a pest in response to some action by people."

It's nice to know we've been having some living biocontrol agents protecting the fruit trees in the garden from mite attacks all along! 😄

description:
Quoting from the original Facebook post: https://www.facebook.com/share/p/1BpEUpHHWP

Fascinating goings on at our aphid-covered rose bush. 

There is so much going on here! We were amazed to read how complex the life cycle of an aphid is: https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aphid. Apparently aphid populations can sometimes even be entirely female and each one can give birth to live young who are themselves born pregnant! Apparently it's called "telescoping of generations". How's that for a party trick? 😮

The winged ones are apparently produced under unfavourable or stressful conditions so that they can fly off to a new food source.

From René Laing's posting: https://www.facebook.com/groups/Butterfliesandbugs/permalink/7019964178101022/, and with some help from Warren Keith Dick, the caterpillar-like visitor to the left in the 3rd piccy is possibly an aphid-munching hoverfly larva.

⚠️🚧🚫
Edit1: According to Mark G Wright, these are most likely Green Peach-Aphids, Greenflies or Peach-Potato Aphids - Myzus persicae: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/243745-Myzus-persicae and https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/243745-Myzus-persicae/browse_photos and, although they are both green, these are *not* Potato Aphids - Macrosiphum eiphorbiae: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/53859-Macrosiphum-euphorbiae and https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/53859-Macrosiphum-euphorbiae/browse_photos, since Green Peach-Aphids are "a highly variable species". Thanks for lending a trained eye there Mark! Appearances can certainly be deceptive with these suckers! 😊 
⚠️🚧🚫

Edit2: Well apparently these little things are even more deceptive than one would imagine - thanks to Annari-du-plessis for flagging the ID and Natalie Hernandez* for clarifying that apparently "Myzus persicae doesn't have black siphunculi (the tailpipes): https://influentialpoints.com/Gallery/Myzus_persicae_Peach-potato_aphid.htm
https://influentialpoints.com/Gallery/Macrosiphum_rosae_Rose_aphid.htm."

*Natalie has a B.S. and M.Sc. in Entomology from the University of Wisconsin - Madison (USA) and her graduate research focused on alate aphids.

So it looks as if these little things are in fact Common Rose Aphids, Macrosiphum rosae: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/53633-Macrosiphum-rosae and https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/53633-Macrosiphum-rosae/browse_photos.

"Macrosiphum rosae, the rose aphid, is a species of sap-sucking aphids in the subfamily Aphidinae. They have a world-wide distribution and infest rosebushes as the main host in spring and early summer, congregating on the tips of shoots and around new buds. Later in the summer, winged forms move to other rose bushes, or to a limited number of secondary hosts, before returning to rosebushes to lay eggs in the autumn.

Wingless adults have a spindle-shaped body and are between 1.7 and 3.6 mm long, slender, varying in colour from green to pink and reddish-brown. The antennae and legs are relatively long, and the cauda (tail-like protrusion) is pale. The siphunculi (pair of small backward-pointing tubes on the abdomen) are long, tapered and black, which distinguishes this aphid from Metopolophium dirhodum, the rose-grain aphid, which has pale siphunculi. Winged individuals are between 2.2 and 3.4 mm in length, varying from green to pinkish-brown, and having distinctive black lateral markings.

This aphid mainly overwinters as eggs on roses, but in mild winters, some adults may survive until spring. The eggs hatch in spring into wingless females which reproduce parthenogenetically, and large colonies can quickly develop, being mainly found on the tips of shoots and around flower buds. The heaviest population densities are in June and July in the northern hemisphere, just when the bushes are flowering, and thereafter the populations decline. This is because at this time of year, some winged females develop, which migrate to other rose bushes or to certain secondary hosts such as holly, teasel, valerian, Knautia and scabious. With the onset of autumn, winged males are also produced, the insects return to roses and the eggs are laid.

Rose aphids damage the aesthetic appearance of rosebushes by contorting the flowers and foliage, and by the sticky honeydew they produce, which often provides a surface on which sooty moulds develop."

Quoting from the original Facebook post containing additional video 🎥 footage: https://www.facebook.com/share/p/1AhKZuJwNw

From strange, to stranger...💛🧡💚🤎❣😄

A little while ago we discovered a really bizarre-looking larva on our Lemon tree: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/290835898. Much to our surprise it was actually eating the Lemon 🍋 leaves! 

Joy duToit le Roux and Steve Woodhall told us that it's apparently the larva of a Common Swallowtail: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6986&taxon_id=47225&view=species, maybe even that of a Greenband Swallowtail or Southern Narrow-Banded Malachite, Papilio nireus ssp. lyaeus: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/347039-Papilio-nireus-lyaeus. Thanks Annari du Plessis, Colin Ralston and Andrew Morton for also confirming the ID for us 🙂

We thought that was quite amazing and decided to try to rear it, together with another one we also found nearby, to see what might emerge.

The fascinating caterpillar transformation process, itself, has already been totally worth it!

Here is one of the larvae. 

It looks a bit like a piece of excrement - orange, green black and white, decorated with odd little spines. 

When you get close to the larva, a bright red set of snail-like "horns" suddenly pops out! We sure didn't see *that* one coming! 😄

If the larva stills feels threatened then it raises its upper body into the air and tucks its head under, looking, for all the world, *just* like a fresh deposit! 😄

Quite amazing...

Update: We later got to see 😃 how these larvae developed into glorious velvety-green caterpillars here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/290847738.

Some time later we got to see the first emergent butterfly, a male here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/290854451.

Little mysteries on the Lemon 🍋 tree in Gulu, on the outskirts of East London, Eastern Cape, South Africa 🇿🇦

How impressive is this? 😃

We just saw this peculiar tangle on our ceiling...on closer inspection we saw this! 👀

At first we weren't quite sure whether this little Jumping Spider had gotten hold of a Midge or a Mosquito, but after checking our records we see this must actually be an Inland Floodwater Mosquito, Aedes vexans: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/155387-Aedes-vexans, https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/155387-Aedes-vexans/browse_photos and similar to one we previously found here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/291382380. 

Ironically the record we're referring to is a set of piccies we took of a dead mosquito we found in our bedroom last Winter. We found it dead, not squashed or anything...just lying there...we still wondered what had happened to it? 🤔

It seems the puzzle pieces 🧩 (with eight legs!) are starting to come together! 🖼 😄 

Our tiny household buddies have our full permission to extract their share of the leech-loot back from the mosquitoes - it may sound weird if you think about it, but unlike the situation with the mosquito, we're OK with an indirect blood donation to these respectful spidies! *They* have never bitten us...unlike the mosquitoes, and they sure don't sound as whiney when we're trying to sleep! 

May the spidies get even better at hunting and get the mosquitoes before they get us!

Wow! 😮 And there we see it happening! 👀😃

This morning we were quite surprised to see several little wasps running to, fro and all over this ootheca...

It's actually a Praying Mantis ootheca laid ~26 days ago: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/292025556.

The ovipositing female is possibly a Miomantis sp.: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/207584-Miomantis, https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/207584-Miomantis/browse_photos?quality_grade=any&place_id=6986 and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6986&preferred_place_id=6986&taxon_id=207584&view=species

As seems to be the case with many such egg clusters, this one must have been parasitised by a wasp. 

Although in this case, we didn't get to see the wasp ovipositing her eggs, some time ago we did actually get to see another wasp ovipositing into a similar ootheca. It's quite an astonishing thing to see: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/292021718. 

Since then we observed several instances of parisitoid wasps emerging from their hosts:

Three clutches from parasitised caterpillars: 
1: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/285303943.

2: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/285532516

3: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/292049614.

And one clutch from parasitised Assassin Bug eggs: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/292078246.

As we learned more about these wasps Alan Manson once mentioned that male emergent wasps often hang around in the hopes of intercepting a similarly-emerging female: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/285303943. 

We decided to monitor the ootheca to see if we could actually record this happening...and that's exactly what we saw! 👀

Several newly-emergent wasps keep returning to the ootheca. They seem to be rather territorial, with one of them chasing the others off.

The dominant male seems to secure the ootheca and there it waits...

Before long another wasp starts to emerge (look in the pink encircled region) and it's instantly intercepted! Exactly as Alan described it...

Update: A while later we took another ootheca aside in order to monitor what might emerge and discovered that it was also parasitised: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/292096040. In *that* case at least three Mantises survived, but the emerging wasps looked similar to these ones.

According to Roberto A. Pantaleoni the parasitoid wasps could possibly be a member of the Eupelmidae family: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/176401-Eupelmidae, https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6986&preferred_place_id=6986&taxon_id=176401&view=species, and possibly an Anastatus sp.: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/250195-Anastatus and https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/250195-Anastatus/browse_photos.

"Lettuce (Lactuca sativa) is an annual plant of the family Asteraceae mostly grown as a leaf vegetable. The leaves are most often used raw in green salads, although lettuce is also seen in other kinds of food, such as sandwiches, wraps and soups; it can also be grilled. Its stem and seeds are sometimes used; celtuce (asparagus lettuce) is one variety grown for its stems, which are eaten either raw or cooked. In addition to its main use as a leafy green, it has also gathered religious and medicinal significance over centuries of human consumption. Europe and North America originally dominated the market for lettuce, but by the late 20th century the consumption of lettuce had spread throughout the world. In 2023, world production of lettuce (and chicory) was 28 million tonnes, led by China with 53% of the total.

Lettuce was originally farmed by the ancient Egyptians, who transformed it from a plant whose seeds were used to obtain oil into an important food crop raised for its succulent leaves and oil-rich seeds. Lettuce spread to the Greeks and Romans; the latter gave it the name lactuca, from which the English lettuce is derived. By 50 AD, many types were described, and lettuce appeared often in medieval writings, including several herbals. The 16th through 18th centuries saw the development of many varieties in Europe, and by the mid-18th century, cultivars were described that can still be found in modern gardens.

Generally grown as a hardy annual, lettuce is easily cultivated, although it requires relatively low temperatures to prevent it from flowering quickly. It can be plagued by numerous nutrient deficiencies, as well as insect and mammal pests, and fungal and bacterial diseases. L. sativa crosses easily within the species and with some other species within the genus Lactuca. Although this trait can be a problem to home gardeners who attempt to save seeds, biologists have used it to broaden the gene pool of cultivated lettuce varieties.

Contaminated lettuce is often a source of bacterial, viral, and parasitic outbreaks in humans, including E. coli and Salmonella.

Lactuca sativa is a member of the Lactuca (lettuce) genus and the Asteraceae (sunflower or aster) family. The species was first described in 1753 by Carl Linnaeus in the second volume of his Species Plantarum. Synonyms for L. sativa include Lactuca scariola var. sativa, L. scariola var. integrata and L. scariola var. integrifolia. L. scariola is itself a synonym for L. serriola, the common wild or prickly lettuce. L. sativa also has many identified taxonomic groups, subspecies and varieties, which delineate the various cultivar groups of domesticated lettuce. Lettuce is closely related to several Lactuca species from southwest Asia; the closest relationship is to L. serriola, an aggressive weed common in temperate and subtropical zones in much of the world.

The Romans referred to lettuce as lactuca (lac meaning "milk" in Latin), an allusion to the white substance, latex, exuded by cut stems. The name Lactuca has become the genus name, while sativa (meaning "sown" or "cultivated") was added to create the species name. The current word lettuce, originally from Middle English, came from the Old French letues or laitues, which derived from the Roman name. The name romaine came from the variety of lettuce grown in the Roman papal gardens, while cos, another term for romaine lettuce, came from the earliest European seeds of the type from the Greek island of Kos, a center of lettuce farming in the Byzantine period."

Wasps! 😮

A while ago we decided to rear a few green caterpillars which had been eating our lettuces: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/292038180.

After a great deal of munching the caterpillars rolled themselves in some lettuce leaves and stitched themselves in with a tiny bit of silk. 

After a while the first caterpillar changed into a beautiful moth, possibly an Essex Y, Cornutiplusia cf. circumflexa: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/292042810.

We waited and waited, but nothing seemed to happen with the other caterpillars. Finally we decided to have a look at one of the rolled lettuce pupae. This is what we found. 

It looks as if there must have been tiny wasps escaping unnoticed from the box every time we opened it. They must have emerged from this dried pupa. The caterpillar must clearly have been parasitised before we started rearing it.

We previously reported on the parasitisation of Scar Bank Gem moth caterpillars by two different types of wasps here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/285291566 (well over 50 black wasps, each about 2.5mm long with long antennae, per cocoon cluster per caterpillar) and here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/285532516 (in excess of a thousand black wasps, each about 3/4mm long with shorter antennae, from one caterpillar).

This parisitisation is different once again. The number of wasps which emerged from this Essex Y moth caterpillar must only have been a handful or they would not have escaped our notice. As was the case with the thousand wasp parasitisation previously mentioned, here there are no tiny wasp cocoons in evidence and the caterpillar body has been entirely consumed. 

The body of this wasp is about 1.5mm long and the antennae are more or less the same length as the length of the body. Interestingly this wasp seems to have a shiny metallic abdomen and a reddish head and thorax with dark markings as seen from above.

Edit: According to Alan Manson this is a Braconid wasp: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6986&taxon_id=63187&view=species and https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/63187-Braconidae. Thanks Alan 🙂 

"The larvae of most braconids are internal or external primary parasitoids of other insects, especially the larval stages of Coleoptera, Diptera, and Lepidoptera, but also some hemimetabolous insects such as aphids, Heteroptera, or Embiidina. Most species kill their hosts, though some cause the hosts to become sterile and less active. Parasitoidy on adult insects (particularly on Hemiptera and Coleoptera) also occurs...Braconids are often used as biological pest control agents, especially against aphids."

A look at a stealth wasp in Gulu, on the outskirts of East London, Eastern Cape, South Africa 🇿🇦

Wow! 👀

We recently brought this Praying Mantis ootheca in from the garden (https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/292103994), in the hopes that we could potentially keep it from being completely parasitised as we had recently found to be the case with a similar one we found on our water tank: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/292029825.

A few days ago some life started emerging...first a few parasitoid wasps and then three dinky Praying Mantises followed by another 40 wasps to date...

Here we have a video of one of the wasps, possibly a male, running around on the ootheca, waiting for a female wasp to emerge (videos in the original Facebook post - link above - piccies extracted from videos). 

The remaining footage is of one of the surviving dinky Mantises 🤗

Edit: According to Roberto A Pantaleoni the parasitoid wasp could possibly be a member of the Eupelmidae family: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/176401-Eupelmidae, https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6986&preferred_place_id=6986&taxon_id=176401&view=species, and possibly an Anastatus sp.: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/250195-Anastatus and https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/250195-Anastatus/browse_photos.

"Eupelmidae is a family of parasitic wasps in the superfamily Chalcidoidea. The larvae of the majority are primary parasitoids, commonly on beetle larvae, though many other hosts are attacked, including spiders. Details of the life history varies considerably (e.g., some attack eggs and others are hyperparasites). They are found throughout the world in virtually all habitats.

They are somewhat variable in appearance, though a fair number of species are relatively easy to separate from other Chalcidoidea by the possession of a medially concave mesonotum [the dorsal (upper) portion of the mesothorax (the middle part of the thorax) of an insect]. They also have the unusual tendency to arch the body strongly upwards when dead, with the head and metasoma often nearly touching above the thorax."

"Anastatus is a large genus of parasitic wasps belonging to the family Eupelmidae. The genus has cosmopolitan distribution."  

Interestingly the wasps that emerged from this ootheca look similar to those that emerged from another ootheca we saw a while ago here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/292029825. Those may consequently be of a similar type to these, unlike the other wasp with enlarged back legs we previously saw parasitising another Praying Mantis ootheca here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/292021718.

Edit2: According to stuffinabox the tiny mantises are indeed also Miomantis sp. as we surmised above: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/207584-Miomantis, https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/207584-Miomantis/browse_photos?quality_grade=any&place_id=6986 and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6986&preferred_place_id=6986&taxon_id=207584&view=species. Thanks for the confirmation stuffinabox! 🙂

Another interesting thing we noticed from the iNat observations recorded for this wasp by CHIK SUI LUN e.g.:  https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/217234643, is that the Praying Mantis ootheca in *that* observation is also redish-pink inside like some of the ones we've been finding here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/292100274, here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/292103994 (the underside of the present one) and here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/292021718. We wonder if this colouration of the inner ootheca could be diet-related or could it be specific to a particular type of Mantis? 🤔

We asked stuffinabox about the different colours of the insides of the oothecas. We had noticed masses of red Soapberry Bugs that had been in the area in the previous months where we found the blood red ootheca.

stuffinabox responded "From what I've seen with Miomantis sp., the colour of the interior harder material is typically an orange-red colour. Even when raised on a diet of insects containing no vibrant pigments, it remains the same.

Difference in colour is more likely species related. Can't say with any certainty though as it's not something I've paid too much attention to." Thanks stuffinabox! That's really helpful 🙂

"The lemon (Citrus × limon) is a species of small evergreen tree in the Citrus genus of the flowering plant family Rutaceae. A true lemon is a hybrid of the citron and the bitter orange. The yellow fruit of the lemon tree is used throughout the world, primarily for its juice. The pulp and rind are used in cooking and baking. The juice of the lemon is about 5–6% citric acid, giving it a sour taste. This makes it a key ingredient in drinks and foods such as lemonade and lemon meringue pie.

The lemon tree produces a pointed oval yellow fruit. Botanically this is a hesperidium, a modified berry with a tough, leathery rind. The rind is divided into an outer colored layer or zest, which is aromatic with essential oils, and an inner layer of white spongy pith. Inside are multiple carpels arranged as radial segments. The seeds develop inside the carpels. The space inside each segment is a locule filled with juice vesicles.

Lemons contain many phytochemicals, including polyphenols, terpenes, and tannins. Their juice contains slightly more citric acid than lime juice (about 47 g/L), nearly twice as much as grapefruit juice, and about five times as much as orange juice."

description:
Quoting from the original Facebook post containing additional video 🎥 footage: https://www.facebook.com/share/p/1QuqLCkuvK

Wow! 😃

We recently discovered masses of these beautiful brown bugs, and even got to see what must be a pair of male and female nymphs.

Amazingly we finally got to see the adults feeding on some little green seeds - what a sight! The hairy seeds stick to absolutely everything - we were completely covered in them after filming, and spent ages picking them off our clothing. Since we involuntarily ended up with so many, we decided to open one up to see what the inner yumminess looks like. It actually looks quite soft and young pea-like in texture...and yes...we had a tiny nibble to see what it tastes like! 😄 It *does* actually taste a bit sweet, like a tiny fresh pea! Who would have guessed...apparently the bugs did! 😁 See the passive partner plant observation link below...

It was all finally worth it to see these bugs eating! The loooong proboscis almost looks like the upper part of a bagpipe and there seem to be two parts...😄

This is apparently a Broad-Headed Bug (Alydidae family): https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6986&taxon_id=62059&view=species and https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/62059-Alydidae.

It's possibly a Riptortus sp.: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/357846-Riptortus and https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/357846-Riptortus/browse_photos. Thanks for confirming the ID for us Dawid Jacobs, Colin Ralston and Johan Pretorius 🙂

It looks similar to a Bean Bug, Riptortus cf. pedestris*: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/357851-Riptortus-pedestris and https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/357851-Riptortus-pedestris/browse_photos. The nymphs look similar to the ones recorded here: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/357851-Riptortus-pedestris/browse_photos?term_id=1&term_value_id=5.

*As pointed out by Dawid, however, "Riptortus pedestris is an Asian species." Thanks for this helpful observation Dawid 🙂

"Alydidae, commonly known as broad-headed bugs, is a family of true bugs very similar to the closely related Coreidae (leaf-footed bugs and relatives). There are at least 60 genera and 300 species altogether. Distributed in the temperate and warmer regions of the Earth, most are tropical and subtropical animals; for example Europe has a mere 10 species, and only 2 of these occur outside the Mediterranean region...

Broad-headed bugs are up to 10–12 millimetres long, and have slender bodies. Some have long and very thin legs. The most notable characteristics of the family are that the head is broad, often similar in length and width to the pronotum and the scutellum, and that the last antennal segments are elongated and curved. The compound eyes are globular and protruding, and they also have ocelli. The femora of the hindlegs bear several strong spines; the tarsus has three segments...

Alydidae are generally of dusky or blackish coloration. The upperside of the abdomen is usually bright orange-red. this color patch is normally not visible as it is covered by the wings; it can be exposed, perhaps to warn would-be predators of these animals' noxiousness: They frequently have scent glands that produce a stink considered to be worse than that of true stink bugs (Pentatomidae). The stink is said to smell similar to a bad case of halitosis...

These bugs mainly inhabit fairly arid and sandy habitat, like seashores, heathland, steppe and savannas. Their main food is seeds, which they pierce with their proboscis to drink the nutritious fluids contained within. Some are economically significant pests, for example Leptocorisa oratoria on rice."

"Desmodium incanum, also known as creeping beggarweed, Spanish clover, Spanish tick-trefoil or hitchhikers is a perennial plant native to Central and South America. A solo visit after four days of frequent all-day rain; I simply had to get out somewhere, 
and I had not visited Perry Oldenburg in at least two months. I walked a unique path today: the west fenceline to the south fenceline, then northeast under the powerline to the east-west trail that continues east from Yes Dear Lane, then south along the east fenceline, cross country (through recent burns) to the nature trail, clockwise, under the powerline to continue along the southern nature trail to the lake, then along its eastern side to the northern nature trail back to Little Red. The weather at the start (1112) was overcast, 88 degrees ("feels like" 100, with probably 95% humidity), with a light breeze. The weather was the same when I left at 1421. Several observations: (1) There were 20 or more cocoons on the western barbed-wire fenceline; iNat's AI identified them as Southern Flannel Moths (Megalopyge opercularis), which makes sense. (2) Several dozen butterflies (swallowtails including many Zebra Swallowtails, Zebra Longwing, Gulf Fritillary, Southern Dogface, and duskywings) were nectaring abundantly on Florida Pusley (Richardia scabra) at the very southwestern corner of the preserve; I was not aware it was such a butterfly plant. (3) It was a great mushroom/fungus day, with hundreds of individuals of many species (too bad most will never be RGed). (4) Clusterspike False Indigo (Amorpha herbacea) is just starting to bloom. (5) Manyflower Beardtongue (Penstemon multiflorus) is blooming abundantly under the powerline. (6) The trail along the powerline is growing up with grasses and forbs; I found no tiger beetles here (although I found two elsewhere). (7) Florida False Sunflower (Phoebanthus grandiflorus) was blooming over much of the preserve, especially along the southern nature trail west of the powerline. (8) About every third Florida False Sunflower bloom had an Orange Blister Beetle (Nemognatha piazata) on it. (9) Sand Post Oak (Quercus margaretiae) has very attractive leaves when young; I photographed several in a recently-burned area. (10) The lake is finally receding after being formed in October 2024 following the passage of one or two hurricanes. Dozens of flooded Slash Pine skeletons dot the former boundary. (11) I probably got some lifer plants; I can't think of any insect that might be a lifer, and I saw very few spiders or vertebrates (although three Green Anoles was nice).

These are my cell-phone photographs (representing 226 records), all time-stamped and geolocated.

Quoting from the original Facebook post: https://www.facebook.com/share/p/1JPaJY6wQx

A fascinating glimpse into the world of a caterpillar moulting, resting and recovering on our Grapevine...what will it become we wonder? (Possibly a Hawkmoth - Sphingidae? 🤔)

1 - Shedding the old skin including the long spiky tail bit (or horn)...
2 - Close up with a finger for scale...the new horn is small and pale
3 - Even the head is looking a bit pale after squeezing out...
4 - Stretching out front view...from back to front: anal prolegs and plate, 4 sets of abdominal prolegs and 3 sets of even smaller thoracic legglets
5 - Stretching out side view -  some lovely pink coming in that "tail", the head is fully extended and the spots (or spiracles used for "breathing") are becoming more defined
6 - Two hours later - side view: a lovely sued brown - hanging on with 3 sets of feet and tucking the head in
7 - Other side - cute little hairs (called barbs) on the proleg feet
8 - Five hours later hanging on by one pair of feet - is it going to fall off?! 😮😧
9 - Two days later...still resting...but thankfully holding on again, 😅 it looks as if the skin is becoming more leathery...
10 - One day further - it has finally started to munch on a grape leaf again! 😃 Plump up little caterpillar!
11 - Close-up of the hidden face and front feet 🙃
12 to 17 - A few days later - nice and round 😄

Update: We kept watching the caterpillar for several days, but at some stage it disappeared - we hoped it had moved down to the leaf litter to pupate but couldn't find it anywhere...

What it is we are to become we do not yet know in Gulu, on the outskirts of East London, Eastern Cape, South Africa 🇿🇦

Iain Darbyshire* kindly identified the plant as a Blue Bushviolet, Barleria obtusa: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/427994-Barleria-obtusa, https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/427994-Barleria-obtusa/browse_photos and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/296822088.

"Barleria obtusa, the bush violet, is a species of flowering plant in the family Acanthaceae. It occurs naturally along forest margins in the summer rainfall region of South Africa (Free State, KwaZulu-Natal, and the Northern Provinces) and in Mozambique. It is widely cultivated as a decorative garden shrub.

In tropical Africa, the leaves are cooked as a vegetable, and the plant is used medicinally."

*Dr. Iain Darbyshire is "A research botanist focusing on the plant diversity of Africa and Madagascar, with a specialist interest in Acanthaceae. Also really interested in an amateur way in the UK flora."

Amazingly enough we recently walked past the plant and noticed these gorgeous little buggies! 

Exactly what we had hoped for and more - a whole family! 😍

The adults are resplendent in brown, green, black and white with a vertical stripe on top of the head and a pair of spiky shoulder pads, while the littlees have more of a flat bronze and black thing going on. These bugs' attire was all the rage in the 80s! 🤗🤭

It looks as if these bugs are members of the Pentatominae subfamily: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/51276-Pentatominae and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6986&preferred_place_id=6986&taxon_id=51276&view=species.

"Pentatominae is a subfamily of Pentatomidae, a family of shield bugs. This subfamily is the largest one within the Pentatomidae, having 4937 species classified in 938 genera. Species in this subfamily are phytophages and several of them are considered agricultural pests. Some invasive pentatomines such as Halyomorpha halys and Bagrada hilaris have been considered household pests."

"Gynenica is a genus of stink bug with about fourteen species in the Afrotropical and Oriental regions. It is one of four genera placed in the tribe Lestonocorini along with Lestonocoris, Neogynenica, and Umgababa that occur in Africa and India and feed on plants in the family Acanthaceae. Bugs in the genus have the pronotum tips extended into forward and upward curving spines. "Belonogaster (belone - "needle", gaster - "belly") is a large genus of mainly Afrotropical quasisocial wasps, although some species occur in Arabia and two extend as far as India. They have characteristics of both the eusocial and the solitary wasps. Belonogaster constructs communal paper nests where the larvae are fed on masticated, soft-bodied insects such as caterpillars. The type species is Belonogaster juncea, which consists of two subspecies: Belonogaster juncea colonialis and Belonogaster juncea juncea. Belanogaster wasps are an important food source for wintering European honey buzzards (Pernis apivorus) in sub-Saharan Africa. In African traditional medicine, wasps of the genus are cooked with plant roots and consumed to cure various childhood sicknesses, as well as having ceremonial use similar to that of honey bees (Apis mellifera). Some birds choose to build their nests near the nests of Belonogaster for protection, including mousebirds and weavers."

"Belonogaster juncea is a typical quasisocial paper wasp from sub-saharan Africa and south-western Asia. It is the type species for the genus Belonogaster.

The nest is similar in form to that of the Polistes paper wasp's nest and is started in a similar way. However, as B. juncea is quasisocial no foundress wasp becomes a dominant queen and all foundresses are full egg-layers, as are any daughters which can mate with males and then join the nest working and laying alongside their mothers. In Cameroon, B. juncea juncea mostly nests in buildings, but nests nave been constructed in the shelter of large boulders. Nests were started throughout the year either by a single female or by groups of two to eight females. Predation and disease meant that only half of the colonies in one study produced at least one adult offspring, and only 10% were able to produce males from the 15% that managed to rear any sexual individuals.

When the original foundress disappears the remaining females fight for dominance, leading to a reduction in breeding success. Almost half of the surviving nests are then abandoned and the average colony lasts about seven months. In a small minority of nests, some females remained on the nest and began a new colonial cycle illustrating semi-independence between colony and nesting cycles. The maximum number of successive cycles to be completed in the same nest was four. The queens of B. juncea therefore demonstrate serial polygyny.

Studies of B. juncea have discerned four behavioural roles for individual adult wasps in a colony. Reproduction is reserved to one individual and the "workers"’ are divided into foragers, builders and guards. The foragers are females that spend the majority of their time foraging to supply the nest with prey and water. Builders are individuals that will bring wood pulp to the nest and then use it to repair or expand the nest. Guards are those females that spend most of their time being inactive on the nest to defend it and its contents from threats.

It ranges through most of Africa south of the Sahara, from Senegal in the west to Ethiopia in East Africa and south to South Africa, including the island of Zanzibar. It also occurs in Asia as far east as India."

Some time ago we discovered a colony of Belonogaster wasps had set up a nest in our garden: https://www.facebook.com/groups/Butterfliesandbugs/permalink/8598204316943659/?app=fbl.

A while later we had a closer look at how the little ones were being "bottle-fed" with mulched up caterpillar balls: https://www.facebook.com/groups/Butterfliesandbugs/permalink/8653329038097853/?app=fbl and the nest cells were being constructed: https://www.facebook.com/groups/Butterfliesandbugs/permalink/8682648151832608/?app=fbl.

We wondered where the wasps were collecting the material for making the nests and thought we could possibly try to follow them around. Easier said than done! The wasps we followed always seemed to be on the hunt for food so we thought we would probably never find out...

Then we noticed this wasp on a Guava leaf...

It's just the answer we've been looking for! 😄 Here (see the Facebook video link above) one of the wasps is carefully scraping off some of the "bum fluff" from one of the leaves. If you look carefully you can even see a remnant ball left behind. Presumably the wasp has ingested the rest and will mix it with saliva to form a ball of cellulosey building material. How amazing! 🙂🤗

Some time ago we also saw a caterpillar similarly munching on the "bum fluff" on a leaf in the bush, Mark G Wright commented that it looked as if the caterpillar was "mowing the trichomes": https://www.facebook.com/groups/Butterfliesandbugs/permalink/8408247685939324/?app=fbl.

A covering of any kind of hair on a plant is an indumentum, and the surface bearing them is said to be pubescent." (https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichome)

So then wasps are effectively mowing the trichomes on the pubescent Guava leaves and combining the "lawnmower cuttings" with saliva to form a ball.

Some time later we realised that this must have been exactly the same behaviour we had previously, many months earlier, seen with another wasp on an Aubergine leaf here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/297824148.

The wasp is a Needle-waisted Paper Wasp, Belonogaster sp.: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/346053-Belonogaster and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=6986&preferred_place_id=6986&taxon_id=346053&view=species.

It's possibly a Belonogaster juncea: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/1070939-Belonogaster-juncea, https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/1070939-Belonogaster-juncea/browse_photos and https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/2359192#page/67/mode/1up

The Northern armyworm, Oriental armyworm or Rice ear-cutting caterpillar (Mythimna separata) is a major pest of maize in Asia.

Nematodes too are pests of maize. It is likely that every maize plant harbors some nematode parasites, and populations of Pratylenchus lesion nematodes in the roots can be "enormous". The effects on the plants include stunting, sometimes of whole fields, sometimes in patches, especially when there is also water stress and poor control of weeds."fuelleborni/browse_photos.

Some time ago we discovered a colony of Belonogaster wasps had set up a nest in our garden: https://www.facebook.com/groups/Butterfliesandbugs/permalink/8598204316943659/?app=fbl.

A while later we had a closer look at how the little ones were being "bottle-fed" with mulched up caterpillar balls: https://www.facebook.com/groups/Butterfliesandbugs/permalink/8653329038097853/?app=fbl and the nest cells were being constructed: https://www.facebook.com/groups/Butterfliesandbugs/permalink/8682648151832608/?app=fbl.

We wondered where the wasps were collecting the material for making the nests and thought we could possibly try to follow them around. Easier said than done! The wasps we followed always seemed to be on the hunt for food so we thought we would probably never find out...

Then we noticed this wasp on a Guava leaf...

It's just the answer we've been looking for! 😄 Here (see the Facebook video link above) one of the wasps is carefully scraping off some of the "bum fluff" from one of the leaves. If you look carefully you can even see a remnant ball left behind. Presumably the wasp has ingested the rest and will mix it with saliva to form a ball of cellulosey building material. How amazing! 🙂🤗

Some time ago we also saw a caterpillar similarly munching on the "bum fluff" on a leaf in the bush, Mark G Wright commented that it looked as if the caterpillar was "mowing the trichomes": https://www.facebook.com/groups/Butterfliesandbugs/permalink/8408247685939324/?app=fbl.

Thanks to Mark we scurried off to find out what trichomes are...Apparently "Trichomes (/ˈtraɪkoʊmz, ˈtrɪkoʊmz/; from Ancient Greek τρίχωμα (tríkhōma) 'hair') are fine outgrowths or appendages on plants, algae, lichens, and certain protists. They are of diverse structure and function. Examples are hairs, glandular hairs, scales, and papillae. A covering of any kind of hair on a plant is an indumentum, and the surface bearing them is said to be pubescent." (https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichome)

So then wasps are effectively mowing the trichomes on the pubescent Guava leaves and combining the "lawnmower cuttings" with saliva to form a ball.

Some time later we realised that this must have been exactly the same behaviour we had previously, many months earlier, seen with another wasp on an Aubergine leaf here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/297824148.
